utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Toma Fila, appearing with Miss Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic on behalf of Mr. Dokmanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask whether Mr. Dokmanovic can hear me. Can you? Yes. Thank you. So I assume the witness will be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down. Thank you. Mr. Fila, may I remind you that you should please be so kind as to speak slowly and to wait a few seconds before you put the next question, otherwise we cannot follow you. Thank you. DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have even written down for myself a reminder to that effect. Mr. Berghofer, you spent several days in the hospital before 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 18th and 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a room for wounded reservists or JNA members in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about reservists. What do you imply under that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia men who had done their military service could, after five or six years, receive military uniforms in the event of a war so as to be prepared for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And those are the people I consider to be reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are those units within the JNA or are they paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to that system, in Yugoslavia they would be legal. However, now they appeared to be paralegal. Paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, how have you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because only they received uniforms as far as I know these others were not in uniform. I do not know. Maybe somebody was in their command, and then they would be within the JNA, if somebody ordered them to go there, but I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your testimony you said that Dr. Bosanac had became director of the hospital. When Dr. Ivankovic was pushed aside, you said. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. I cannot recall saying that, that Dr. Bosanac was director and that he had been pushed aside. I cannot remember that. Could you please remind me in more detail, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will find it in a moment. On page 3, you said: "Dr. Bosanac became director in the hospital as soon as Dr. Ivankovic had been pushed aside."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, very well. Perhaps I did say that, but I remember that on the night between 19th and 20th, Dr. Bosanac gave -- conveyed a message to Dr. Ivankovic asking him to come to an office and then he said to her, "how come you want me now and for three months you never called me". I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not give me the answer why you use the term, "pushed aside". Was that because he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not my expression. That is not an expression I use.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But that is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not have said that. I may have said that he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I remind you that you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I did, but maybe in the translation when I said that he was replaced they interpreted it as being pushed aside. Maybe the person who was translating instead of putting, "replaced", put, "pushed".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will look at the English version. Since I do not speak English would you please allow my colleague to read it out for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "Dr. Bosanac became director of the hospital, which had pushed Dr. Ivankovic to one side. She wanted to talk to Mladen because the occupation of the Chetniks..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I must assert that he was replaced. He was dismissed. Let me give you the reason. When we would come to the hospital at times, bringing food, then a nurse called Mandic who is also a Serb, she is in Zagreb now, said, "Mr. Nikola and Drago, in future when you bring something, do not bring it to Dr. Ivankovic but bring it here because he has been replaced". So I would never have used the term, "pushed aside", that he was replaced, yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But why was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you must ask the professionals, I am very good friends with Dr. Ivankovic. I was a friend for 15 or 16 years. I have every appreciation for him still, but why he was replaced I could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your stay in the hospital for three days, 17, 18 and 19, did you see Dr. Dokmanovic anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you were put on the buses. What kind of buses? Military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you were driven to the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But they were not buses from Vukovar. I wish to underline that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What kind of buses were they in terms of colour, licence plate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think the licences were of Zarenijan. They were not very new, but they were not that old either, maybe ten years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were beige, off-white.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you mentioned Professor Licina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did he get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He got off the bus in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A reservist said, "Mr. Licina, how come you are here?" He shrugged his shoulders and five minutes later he was taken out. He, Hidek, and Kolesar, the husband of the head nurse of Dr. Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are quite sure, he was not taken off at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, he was sitting in front of me in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you, did the Serbs start leaving Vukovar before these events when you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are thinking of these two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, before that, June, July, August, September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did go. I cannot say they did not. Others stayed with me in the basement. I can tell you their names. I am still good friends with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, since you said you had a watch when you were in the barracks, about what time did you leave the JNA barracks and at what time did you reach Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I must explain. I had two watches, a wristwatch and a pocket watch, but I think it was around -- do not take me by my word -- but it was about five to one or ten past one in the afternoon. In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you at ten past one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the barracks then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And roughly at what time did you reach Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not drive fast, they drove rather slowly, so roughly half an hour, about 2 pm. I could not really tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But around 2 pm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic during the time when the buses were still being unloaded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean before all the buses had been unloaded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that daytime when visibility is good, was it dusk or was it night-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me add, sir, take into consideration that there were about 240 of us. That is not the exact figure, but roughly, and take into consideration that first our personal documents were seized. Then we were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were saying that the buses were being unloaded. Was that a time when visibility was very good when you saw Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was still complete daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you were later on taken out of the hangar and that you spent some time outside, and then you were taken by a vehicle somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were taken out of the hangar was it still daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was daylight for another roughly 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From the moment you left the hangar, another 40 minutes of daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that, 45 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So when you left it was dark or was it dusk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dusk, but when we reached the main road, Vukovar, Negoslavci, it was completely dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From the moment you left the hangar, did you go back into it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, that from the moment you were taken out of the hangar until you were taken towards Velepromet and wherever, you were outside all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yesterday you described to us how you entered -- and the beatings, and so on. In answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said, "in such situations one sees...", and then you added something else. You used a term that I did not quite catch. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, in such circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were saying something to the effect, you saw... and something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course. One is not indifferent in such circumstances and one is doing one's best to avoid the beatings. I may have added something else but could you remind me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me remind you. You said that one sees things that one does not see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I was hit in the head, the Prosecutor asked me whether I lost consciousness. No. On the contrary. I saw the stars. Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you said, "one sees things that one does not see", under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that your wife was killed by the shelling on 6th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You remember very well that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 6th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How can you explain that in your statement it says that she was killed on 4th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still think it was the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But in your statement you said the 4th. It is an important date, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps she was killed on the 4th and we buried her on the 6th in the hospital, but I still think it was the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are you sure of? Was it the 4th or the 6th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are sure it was the 6th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then please explain why, in your previous statement, you said the 4th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, in many statements the translator may not translate things correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But Mr. Berghofer, you signed that statement. Surely you know what you say and what you sign.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know what I say, but it is not my way to sign things. Maybe here, now, someone may be wrong. There are three dates I remember well. When I got to Ovcara, when I returned from Mitrovica and when that woman was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your statement it says that the statement was read out to you before by the investigator, before you signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you sign it if it was not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I was tired or simply I did not follow carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it occur to you that you mix up dates and times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not so much dates, and some dates I really do not remember but certain specific dates I do remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you said that you knew Dokmanovic only by sight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that Dokmanovic does not know you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you are wrong with dates could you not mix up faces too? Maybe somebody reminded you that this was Dokmanovic. Somebody told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know roughly 20,000 people. I know the names of many. Others I do not. Him I know by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anyone remind you of this? Refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not necessary. I was active in football and I know that he played football too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You lost your daughter, you lost your wife, you lost your property, your life was in jeopardy. You are in a difficult situation. You are being beaten. You cannot remember exactly when your wife was killed. How can you expect me to believe that you will remember a person you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away, it was only in Zagreb that I learned that my daughter was missing. I left and my daughter was in another house. She was married. I left that house on 24th in the night when they fired at it, and I learned that my daughter was missing in 1993, I think. Some people from Vukovar came and said that my daughter was not there, then I thought to myself, "that must be a mistake". I do not know whether that is of any interest to you but let me tell you, I was divorced from their mother in 1981 and this other lady that got killed, I considered her to be my wife, though we were not married. So it was only in 1993 in Zagreb that I learned that my older daughter, who is one year senior to the younger one, was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You had no contact with her until 1993 and you did not look for her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not. There was no communication with Vukovar. It is only now for the past six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But there was the Red Cross and other organisations. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not mention, sir, that while I was in Mitrovica, my mother was in hospital. She fell, being short she had a broken hip and she died. It is something I did not tell you, and who could find one's daughter out of the 300,000 exiles that Croatia had, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned a name called Duvnjak and that someone shot at him. Let me remind you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I am here under oath. I did not say he was shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, maybe I misunderstood. Will you please describe once again what you said to avoid all misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. Around the 19th November, and I must be very careful with the minutes so as not to make any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do not worry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, anyway, on 19th in the afternoon this receptionist from the hospital came. His name is Bogdan Kuzmic. I just remembered, luckily, his name, and he entered a car. From the room I was in I looked out and I saw on a chair this Duvnjak sitting on a chair as a wounded person. He was about 12 metres away from me, and I just heard him shrug his shoulders and say, "what else could I do?". That is all I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you see him for the last time? Was he taken away then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him being taken away. I just saw Kuzmic talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You do not know what happened to him afterwards, this Duvnjak? Is he a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a Croat. He worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that at one point in time you saw Slavko Dokmanovic and you were not quite sure what time it was. It was 2 pm, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was closer to 3 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But it was not 4 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was between 3 and 4 pm. I really cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it daylight and people are still coming off the buses at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us once again what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing. Could you start from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a complete pilot's uniform of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he wearing on his feet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normal regular shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not boots, shoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shoes, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then I assume he was wearing trousers. What colour were the trousers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dark blue, navy blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he had a kind of wind jacket, a wind breaker, a kind of synthetic material. It was not buttoned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are using a local term, "basket jacket", that people do not know. It comes from basketball.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, very well, a wind jacket then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With a zip? How did it button up in front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front. Yes, with a zip. You know what that is, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. So a wind jacket from a nylon material with a zip in front.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. You said it was a nylon wind jacket with a zip in dark blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The suit, the pilot's suit was dark blue. You know that very well, what the pilot's uniform was like in the Yugoslav army. They differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I have understood you, but then the wind jacket with a zip. What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was more like black, but it was still darker, dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he wearing it? Were his hands in the sleeves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing it, but it was not buttoned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you see his shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any insignia on the shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Underneath that wind jacket? He must have been wearing something underneath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was, he was wearing his jacket. Or the blouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And below that blouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A shirt and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shirt was blue. A bit lighter blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he wearing anything on his hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was bareheaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All that time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But while you were looking at him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not looking at him all the time, sir. He was inside. He was maybe inside for four or five minutes, maybe 10 minutes. I pointed out in my statement that I was not sure for how long they were beating this man. Later on I realised it was Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said it was four or five minutes but how long were you looking at him like you are looking at us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, roughly for the same time, same amount of time. I cannot really count the minutes. I cannot tell you with absolute precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well, but throughout that time while you were looking at him, he did not have anything on his head. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he without a hat when he addressed the Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really could not tell you. When I saw him as far as I can remember his cap was attached on his right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Attached to what? Attached to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As if it was in the pocket of his wind jacket. Or maybe at his belt here in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he had a belt too, an army belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a belt, an ordinary belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know the difference, I am asking you whether he had a military belt or an ordinary belt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had an ordinary trouser belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he had the Tito cap which was attached to his belt on his trousers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, in all the statements you made, you never mentioned this Tito cap, nor any wind jacket or basket jacket. Why did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one asked me about Dokmanovic. It was only me, myself who volunteered the information that he was there. There may be other things that one could not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But no one asked you about the wind jacket yesterday and you spoke about it now. How come you did not before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I just did not remember or people did not enquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, how come you mentioned it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no one asked me about shoes yesterday. You did today, so it depends on what questions one is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the statement you made before this tribunal you said that you saw him at 2 pm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I told you that I cannot guess the exact time, but I am quite sure that when we left Ovcara it was getting dark because the lights were switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was when you were leaving, but when you were arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were arriving it was full daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In answer to a question by the Prosecutor you said it was 2 pm. Shall I read it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can read it, yes. We reached Ovcara somewhere around 2 pm, and then it took time for people to get beaten and I told you, that took some time. I do not know why you are so interested in these times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me read it to you: "About 2 pm the reservists..." "The reservist", you said, "Slavko Dokmanovic". Today you said he is a JNA officer: "... who was president of the municipality entered the hangar and said to Emil, 'you are here inspector, too...' "

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I refer whether counsel is referring to the transcript or to a statement because I am sure he said to the witness that it was a transcript of yesterday's proceedings that he was quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, not yesterday's transcript, but the statement of the witness. The statement made to the investigator Mr. Curtis, the same gentleman who arrested Dokmanovic. It is his statement and it is a part of the record, if I have understood well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well if Mr. Fila would allow me, I am merely saying that it should be made clear to the witness that it is not his testimony yesterday, but in his previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is what I said, that I was invoking his statement, and that is what I am reading from. I do not know what page it is though. I will tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, actually, honestly, I too misunderstood you. I thought you were speaking of the transcript, so therefore it was a very good clarification, a point of clarification, so it is clear that you are now mentioning his statement and not the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just to be quite clear, I am talking about two statements. First is the statement he gave to Kevin Curtis, page 7 -- is it 7? Yes. Page 7. It is the penultimate page ... of the translation? Of the translation. Stevan Zoric, Zlatko Gradin are talking, and then he says: "Around 1400 hours the reservists...", et cetera, et cetera. That is what I read. Then there is another statement he gave, which caused this confusion. According to Rule 61, he was speaking before Judge Claude Jorda and after that the indictment followed. This is again the penultimate page. He says: "Around 2 o'clock this afternoon the reservist whom I knew who was president of the municipality, Slavko Dokmanovic, entered the hangar and told Emil..." Et cetera, et cetera. So before he spoke yesterday he made two statements and he said, "before 1400 hours", and that is why I am asking at what time, because time is very important for me and you know why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please do. Is it around 1400 hours as you said before? Or what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, once again, could you read out quite clearly or say what I am supposed to answer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are your two statements true, one that you gave to the investigator, Mr. Curtis, and the other one before the Chamber of Judge Jorda, that this was at 1400 hours, around 1400 hours on 20th November when you saw Slavko Dokmanovic, the reservist, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to what I am saying. I could not look at my watch any more at that point, because I did not have a watch at that point. First of all, you forgot that I lost my watch because Goran Mugosa took it away from me. That is one thing, and secondly, perhaps there is a misunderstanding here. All of them were in JNA reservist uniforms, except that Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing an airman's uniform, a blue uniform. Now listen to me carefully, this reservist, this reservist, what I said, this did not refer to Slavko Dokmanovic because Slavko Dokmanovic has his name and surname and this reservist was a bigger man, but his name is not there because I do not know his name, and that is why I emphasise this, and the, "and the reservist", and this reservist is probably one who had a whistle, so perhaps that is where there is this small misunderstanding. It is not that I called Slavko Dokmanovic a reservist, perhaps the reservist is the one who had a whistle. I am emphasising that there were 11, 12 or 13 of them. How can I tell in two groups? One was indoors, one was outdoors and then a reservist walked in, and he blows a whistle and he says, "that is enough". One group gets out but what does that matter because another group walks in, so again, I imagine it is this lack of understanding that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, let us not continue this. Could the witness himself read what he said to Mr. Curtis, and then at the hearing before Judge Jorda? In both areas he said that Slavko Dokmanovic is a reservist and that this is at 1400 hours and now before you he said that this was not so. The only way in which we can ascertain what he said is in this way, I think. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. This question has been asked and answered at least three or four times. The witness has given his explanation. Mr. Fila has made it clear that the transcript of the 61 hearing and of the statement is apparently inconsistent with that. That has been made clear. That is the end of the matter, your Honours. We could go on for the next week doing this but we will get no further. The question has been asked and has been answered and I object to any further questions on the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, however, I do not see anything against just asking the -- anything against the motion by the Defence counsel. I do not see why the witness should not be allowed to just read out the two lines to which Defence counsel is referring and then we will move on to a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why do you not give the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, could he read his statement in the Serbian, the Croat language which he speaks? This is page 7. This section up to here. Just one line. One line. Please read exactly what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. All right. I do not see that there is any problem involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read it. And so, after all Slavko Dokmanovic is a reservist too, but if I understood Mr. Fila correctly, or perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps did he not understand me. Perhaps could you read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no problem, yes: "Around 1400 hours the reservist Slavko Dokmanovic who was president of the municipality..."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing else is needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see any -- well, I mean, you are an expert so you know, but for me he is a reservist too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "For me he is a reservist too". Two minutes ago you said he was not a reservist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, come on sir, Mr. Fila, I do not know how old he is and if he does not belong to the regular army in our country in Yugoslavia, it was called a reservist. He was over 25 years of age and he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If it means anything to you, there was never an airman's uniform of the kind you are describing in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my service in the Yugoslav army, and I can tell you that this uniform exists until the present day. Please explain to the honourable judges what a Yugoslav airman's uniform is like, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There are quite a few differences, you know. I do not want to tire the court with that any longer. For example, yesterday you say between 19th and 20th between 1:15 and 3:15 gunshots were heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in your statement before Kevin Curtis you said that a few bursts of gunfire were heard. There is a difference, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you know very well what bursts of gunfire are. That is from an automatic rifle and I am telling you again, I cannot guess the exact minute, but I can tell you that 18 shots from one pistol were fired in about an hour or two, but with a short break. Six bullets is one pistol, but that is one pistol, not one burst of gunfire because, you see, there can be these mistakes that the interpreters or translators make and a burst of gunfire is from an automatic rifle so you cannot tell how many shots are being fired but from a pistol when you hear this whistling sound, six of them, and then there is a break of 40 or 50 minutes -- again, please do not ask me exactly what the minutes involved were but again, you could hear from -- from the same pistol you could hear six bullets and then again six.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I really do not understand you. I am saying what you said in your statement, "a few bursts of gunfire", and yesterday you said, "shots from a pistol". These several bursts of gunfire of 18 bullets and shots from a pistol, is that all the same to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you know what the mistake is there? Many of these translators, perhaps it is all the same to them whether we are talking about burst of gunfire, individual shots, but you know exactly what a burst of gunfire is and you know that individual shots are not a burst of gunfire, so what I am telling you now is from a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what you said in the statement, "a few burst of gunfire of 18", is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It is from one identical pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry for tiring you, honourable judges, but we are trying to ascertain how reliable the witness is. I am going to read something else from his statement. Yesterday you said that Slavko Dokmanovic came in five or six minutes after you. Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And first he hit a wounded man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dado Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then he hit a little boy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you said that this was the son of Baumgartner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure but I did not know the boy, but his father was looking for him so, you know. Even now I am not too sure it is the young Baumgartner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you mean, "I am not too..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was simply a young boy of 17 or 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it Baumgartner or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Fila, I was not sure yesterday and I am not sure today that this is Baumgartner. The other day I came to realise what it was, but it was a young man and I cannot guarantee it is Baumgartner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the statement you made to Mr. Curtis you do not mention this young boy at all. How come the young boy appeared just now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I made this statement and it was not put in. I tell you, many of these translators, if they are not translating well, it is only natural that I get into this kind of situation. There is something wrong, but what is correct is what I am telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you also said that after that, first he hit the wounded man, then the young boy and then Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not hit Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then he said, "where are you, inspector"? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is the sequence correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, "Oh, Mr. Inspector, you are here too".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the 61(B) hearing, you said first he hit the young boy and then the wounded man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. First Dado Dukic, who I know very well, and then he hit the young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is your statement at the Rule 61(B) hearing. You said: "First the young man and then him."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am telling you once again, you know that many of these things depend on the translator and interpreters. Perhaps it was all the same to the translator whom -- state first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is a transcript from the hearing. It is not that he puts someone first or second, what is translated is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you think that now perhaps no mistakes are being made in what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I apprehend that the witness is confused as to what transcripts are being referred to. It may be that the witness has no idea what a Rule 61 transcript is. It is unfair to put questions to the witness if he is confused and does not understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I appeal to Mr. Fila maybe to move on to other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the statement you made to Mr. Curtis, you know that you gave a statement to Mr. Curtis and you know what I am talking about. Please tell me, you said that first he greeted Cakalic , "Oh, you are here too, inspector", and then he hit the wounded man and you did not mention the young man at all. How do you explain that? I hope that you know what I am referring to now so that the Prosecutor would not have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen, let me tell you. I am claiming now, too, that first he hit Dado Dukic and then when he hit him, he hit his head against the wall and the man screamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am speaking of the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I have my own order. If the translator places one name first and another name second it is not my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With your permission I shall read this to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am sorry, can you tell us what you are going to read now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, now I am going to read the transcript of the Rule 61 hearing from the 27th March 1996 on page -- it is the Serbian translation, the Croatian translation so it is hard to tell. Now, you said: "Since I was in the fifth bus which was the penultimate one, when I enter the hangar, when I ran into it I saw a young man running into the hangar after me. He was moving in the same direction as Dokmanovic was, and he looked quite nervous. He had his hands on his back. He was walking up and down in the hangar and when this young man ran by him, he jumped up like a football player and he managed to hit the young man in the face with his foot, so he kicked the young man in the face." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I shall continue: "About 10 minutes later, or perhaps a bit less, Dr. Dado Dukic was there. Dado Dukic was wounded in the legs. He was huddling by the wall and Dokmanovic came and kicked him a volley." You remember what a volley in soccer football is. Do you understand that this differs from what you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can I answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please do, that is why I am reading it out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Listen to me, you see where the mistake is? It is not Dr. Dado Dukic, it is the son of Dr. Dukic. The son of Dr. Dukic, Dado Dukic. Do you see where the mistake is? I am telling you again. If a translator cares about every letter and if a translator is not very careful, a mistake can be made. As far as this young man is concerned, you used something different. I was already in the hangar when the young man was running in. It is not that the young man was running after me. I was already in the hangar when the young man ran into the hangar by Slavko Dokmanovic. It is very simple in soccer football. You call it scissors, you know, when he jumps up with both legs. So that is how the young man was moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am just trying to tell you that there are differences in your statements and in the order ascertained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, Dr. Dukic, he was not a doctor. It was not Dr. Dukic who was there. That is why I have to amend this. Perhaps I did not know -- perhaps this translator, you know, there are different translators. Now, you and I did not know what a "suska" was, a synthetic wind jacket was, and now the gentlemen here do not know what a wind breaker is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Oh yes, a basketball jacket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You know, this was an expression we used in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes of course I know it, but I am talking about the order. It is not important whether Dado Dukic is a doctor or not. It is the order that you have been changing from one statement to another. You have been giving a different order, a different sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not perplexed at all, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, now, you have made your point and with all due respect I would like to, again, call upon you to move on to a different question. It is very clear. You have made your point, your objection, the witness has given us an account of what happened according to him and we can now, as I say, move on to a different point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, just a minute, please. I am just trying to check whether I have forgotten something. I think I will be finished very soon. Definitely, I am only interested in the order of the buses. What bus were you on, who was sitting front of you, who was sitting behind you and do you know where Cakalic was sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Fila. I have to go back in time about seven years now, right? You see, many people have lost their lives, and now you are asking me where I was sitting. I am overjoyed to have remembered that Hidek was with me, that Professor Licina was with me, and Nurse Biba's husband. What would happen if I never knew them, just like I did not know many people at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Not to keep you much longer, we are all pretty tired now, was Cakalic with you on the same bus and where was he and where was he sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember he was on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the same bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, let me think. Yes, yes, as far as I can remember, in the same bus. In the barracks I was on the left-hand side, the left-hand side, and then when we came I was on the opposite side of the hangar in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you about the bus and what bus it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the fourth bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because in your statements it says the fifth or the sixth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were six buses altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said the third and the fifth and the sixth and now you have said the fourth bus. And Cakalic was with you on the same bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and Damjan Samardzic too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I am interested in Cakalic. Another thing, the paramilitaries you saw in the hospital. Did they go to the barracks and to Ovcara too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Or did these people change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the next day the regular army was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps we did not understand each other correctly. On the 20th when you were taken out of the hospital, and when you were boarding the buses, I am talking about the paramilitaries, you are arriving at the barracks and then you go to Ovcara. Did you notice that these were the same people, the same faces at all three key points, namely the hospital, the barracks and Ovcara? Among others, I mean...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you know, when it is easy, it is easy, when I know someone, and then I can tell whether he is a paramilitary. I only saw Bogdan Kuzmic there in a uniform of a JNA reservist, and then I simply did not see these other people whom I did not know. I really do not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you returned to Velepromet, this is truly my last question, did you see people in civilian clothes, perhaps? People from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. First of all, I saw the mother of Goran Mugosa Kustro. She was the first one, she is my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Goran Kustro is the one who took your money, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Mugosa Kustro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about him yesterday. He took your money.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, his mother. She is a neighbour by the store.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The one who took your money and not your watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took the watch too, but accidentally the pocket watch stayed. I imagine he had had enough. I did not really have that much money.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, that will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, when you were answering Mr. Fila's questions about times, particularly at the JNA barracks and then subsequently at the Ovcara farm, were you giving Mr. Fila your best estimate of the times as you can now recall them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila also asked you questions about you being taken out of the hangar and I think you said when you went outside it was light. How long did you stay outside the hangar before you got on to the combi-bus which took you back into Vukovar? Can you remember? If you cannot remember it does not matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I remember quite well. This was a Polo car and we were outside for about 35 minutes. Well, you know, it is easiest for me to say when we left, that is, when night falls, around 5 o'clock, but we were outside about 35 minutes or perhaps even 40 minutes. This was before night fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, you were asked a number of questions by Mr. Fila about the clothes that Mr. Dokmanovic was wearing at the time. Is Mr. Dokmanovic's face familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is there any doubt in your mind that the person you saw there at the time was Mr. Dokmanovic? At the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could not happen. That could not happen. Because if you have known a man for over twenty years and, you know, there are some people you cannot remember even if you have seen them three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, do you have any doubt or not? Perhaps you could just answer my question about the man you saw there on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure. I am sure it was Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berghofer, I am sorry, you must be rather tired and of course this may be emotionally involved and so I am so sorry, I need to ask you one or two questions, if you do not mind. The first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement you made when you were interviewed in June 1995, do you remember, by a Tribunal's investigator, at one point, you said, and I quote your words, you said: "Dokmanovic was pacing up and down inside the hangar whilst people were being beaten and I very much got the impression that he was the person in charge there, although I heard him give no orders." Now, how did you make -- this is my question; how did you make this impression, that Mr. Dokmanovic was the person in charge within the hangar? On the basis of what elements or facts did you come to the conclusion that he was the person in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, in a company, a worker has to respect his manager. That is, for example, the difference between myself and Slavko Dokmanovic. There were five steps between us. He was a politician, a top man there. He was president of the municipality. Also, you know, those boys, those reservists that he was there with, I did not hear him issue orders, but my assumption is that if he is the president of the municipality, his word would have been taken for what it is worth, had he said, "do not beat them any more". I did not hear him say a word, issue a single order, and I am telling you now, too, as a person, I could not say all that freely, that he is not all that responsible for everything that happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is your inference, but I, again if you do not mind, I would like to insist on this question. So you said, "my assumption was that he was a person in authority and command", but did you infer this from any, say, gesture made -- from the way he was behaving within the hangar, not outside the hangar, within the hangar. Forget about his previous status, his status as a president of the assembly of Vukovar municipality. Now, try to focus on what he actually did, and on how he behaved in the hangar. Did he behave in such a manner that -- you might infer from that, that he was really in command, that everybody would have followed his orders, had he given orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you again my opinion is that he did have an authority there. I mean, that he did have authority over the reservists. You know, like a boss, like a leader. Personally, if I were in the place of these reservists, I would have acted the same way, because I respect people who are above me. I think that he did have an authority of his own over them if this is clear to you, but if I did not respond properly, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, thank you. Thank you for your answer, and if you do not mind, I move to my second and last question. Now, when you were, as you said in your statement, saved, so taken out of the hangar, separated by somebody from the other people who were inside, you were taken out and were you by yourself or were you in a small group of persons who, like you, had been, "saved", by somebody inside when you were standing outside the hangar after the beating? Were you alone? Or were you in a group of persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (redacted) I would never recognise him again. At that time he was about 18 years old. He was not that tall. And, and, and this (redacted) was there too. I did not recognise him either. I could not remember anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, and when you were with this group of people what happened before you were taken away from that place and transferred to Velepromet? Did you meet or did you get in touch with any JNA officer before you left that place to go by bus or by some sort of van to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I gave these particulars, the name and surname, but I am not too sure any more, honestly. I mean, my knees were shaking but there was someone who was taking our particulars, you know, sir, it is a bit late now, and going back to all this time, but I think that I gave the name and surname. As far as I know, none of them had any insignia of the former Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Were you interrogated by some military person, whether or not he was wearing any insignia, whether or not he was an officer, the group of six or seven people of which you were a member? Was this group interrogated by an officer, or a military man before you boarded the van to go to Velepromet?, if you do not remember, do not worry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we only gave our names and surnames. I personally was not asked a thing. I was just asked what my surname was. I gave my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there is any objection to the witness being released. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would ask that the witness not be released, but there be no constraints on him leaving the jurisdiction, leaving the precincts of the court and returning to Yugoslavia, but whilst the outstanding exhibit is still there, we would ask that he not be formally released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Do you agree? There is a problem. I do not know whether my learned colleague understood me. A name was mentioned that should not have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We ask for a redaction, page 37, line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Berghofer, thank you so much for coming here to testify and you may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am instructed that there is another redaction, please, at page 41, lines 18-21, if your Honours please... your Honours, it may be that there is a confusion between the pages. I think perhaps the Registrar might be able to ascertain that. I think it is probably page 41, 18-21.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is the only redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you going to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would call Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cakalic. May I ask you to make the formal declaration? EMIL CAKALIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In June of 1995, Mr. Cakalic, do you recall meeting with Mr. Vladimir Dzuro, an investigator from the Tribunal Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that time, did you give a statement to him which was taken down in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was that statement subsequently read back to you by an interpreter into the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that time I would ask that the witness be shown this document, please. We would mark this as Prosecutor's exhibit...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: 51. Again, Mr. Cakalic, is that your signature that appears on this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Since you have been in The Hague have you had an opportunity to review a Croatian translation of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In doing so, did you find two minor errors which you would like to correct at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am going to direct you to page 5 of the Croatian version of the statement, paragraph 4, and can you tell me if you see the errors that you have recognised? And your Honours, the corresponding spot in the English version is in the last paragraph on page 5. Have you found the errors that you have pointed out previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a question of the strength of the glasses, so it should be 1:25 on top, and 2:75 for the lower part of the glasses. The figures should be inverted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is there anything else in that same paragraph which you felt needed to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It should have said , "he was president of Vukovar municipality and a member of the Serbian National Council". The word, "national", has been omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Having clarified those two points is your statement otherwise correct and true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would then tender the English version of the statement as Prosecutor's Exhibit 51 and the Croatian version as Prosecutor's Exhibit 51A, both under sale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, what about the supplement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am getting to that at this point, your Honour. I was going to tender that as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A question please, your Honour. What about the supplement that I received last night, is this part of this exhibit or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, I am going into that right now. I will tender that under a separate exhibit number just for the purposes of clarity, so if one of them is being referred to, we all know which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, in April of 1996 did you again meet with Mr. Dzuro in order to give a brief supplement to your earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was this statement also taken down in the English language but read back to you in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness this document, and I will mark this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 52. Do you recognise your signature on the English version of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review a Croatian translation of this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you believe that it is correct and true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would then tender this supplemental statement as Prosecutor's Exhibit 52 and the Croatian translation of it as Prosecutor's Exhibit 52A, both under seal. Mr. Cakalic, in May of 1992 were you interviewed by the Croatian police at the main police station in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was a report or I think correctly termed, "an official note", made pursuant to that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That note was made but I had not seen it before. The note is a document intended for official persons who have knowledge or are familiar with the activities of somebody, and who needs that information for further processing, and which he may use to refresh his memory or to deal with some data in a more precise fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to show Mr. Cakalic this document now, and I believe Mr. Fila will have the same objection that he had yesterday, but we will mark this for identification purposes only. At this point I would mark it as Prosecutor's Exhibit 53, and the English translation of this as 53A. On the last page of the Croatian version of this official note, do you see a signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is the signature of the person who compiled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And that is not your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would tender these now but I understand Mr. Fila would object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila? Do you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I need to repeat my same objection that I had yesterday? I think not. There is no need to waste the court's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, we will mark it for identification as Prosecutor's Exhibit 53 and 53A at this time. Mr. Cakalic, can you tell the court where you are from originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am from Fericanci, a place towards the north about 60 kilometres from Osijek, north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you grow up in Fericanci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fericanci. I lived there until the 2nd February 1943, from my birth until that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did you move in 1943?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Varazdin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point in time did you end up in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. About the middle of December, and I lived there until 1st July 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you were in Zagreb, did you pursue your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I completed secondary school there, and I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you then enter into any higher education after secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, but only after I obtained a job in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what was the job that you obtained in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was head of the central medical laboratory, and the laboratory for blood transfusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what is your training in? What field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed the higher school of sanitary technicians in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you were working as a sanitary technician in Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a sanitary inspector. In 1968 I left the Vukovar hospital and became employed in the municipality of Vukovar as a sanitary inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until, for as long as it was possible, actually, during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this was up until 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. And in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time in early 1991 when barricades were put up in some of the villages around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did this occur, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the killing of Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How would you describe the situation in Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the massacre of Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A rather strained psychological relation developed among the population of Vukovar. After that, the shooting started. People were out of their wits. Some people had one set of information, other people had a different set. I think that psychologically the situation was very grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Over the summer, did the situation improve at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened during the course of the summer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shelling of the town started, by formed paramilitary units. Later, also, by members of the Yugoslav army, who were well-armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the summer did people who lived in Vukovar leave the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many left the city, but many also returned after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge why were people leaving the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that during the summer there started to be shelling of the city. Was the shelling intense at the outset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It first started as sporadic shelling. The shells first fell, as far as I can remember, in the vicinity of the house in which I lived. Then in the centre of town, then the suburbs coming from the direction of Borovo Selo, the fire came from Brsadin. In August these attacks were quite serious. Throughout the day one could hear automatic weapons fire, then planes started attacking and then gradually it turned into real war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you remain at your house during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where was your house located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Boris Kidric Street, number 79. That is near the city stadium in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was anyone with you at your home through the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent very little time at home because I was busy doing my work. There was my wife, there were my neighbours and friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were living conditions like for you and your wife during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same as for everyone else. As far as physical fitness was concerned, the satisfaction of elementary needs like food and water, these were sufficient up to the end of September. Later on there was no running water any more, because the pipes, pipelines of the central water supply system of the city of Vukovar had been damaged, and also some of the surrounding villages. As regards food, it had to be destroyed because it was kept in refrigerators and there was no more electricity, so that we mainly used packed foods or...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that you were away much of the time. Did you have certain duties or responsibilities during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I volunteered and applied to the Secretariat of National Defence to engage in preventative medical activities for the benefit of the Croatian army and police and all the population of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what did this job entail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primarily supply with good quality drinking water for the population and the army, provision of hygienically correct foodstuffs for the Croatian army and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during the time of the battle are you aware of any epidemics or outbreaks of disease in the city under these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They did not happen because I gave very strict instructions, very precise ones as to the way in which the washing and disinfection of all utensils used for the preparation of food and the transportation of food should be done. All the containers before transportation had to be given to me for inspection, and only after that could they be filled with food which other people would have to taste. This was obligatory. And only then was it transported to particular points, and it was always cooked food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time near the end of the battle when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th November my wife and I left our home and went to the Vukovar hospital because we had been informed that units of the Yugoslav army and paramilitary units in the street in which I lived had boarded inhabitants in personnel carriers and taken them away. That same moment my wife and I and our neighbours, mostly Croats, abandoned our homes. Some of us went to the hospital compound. I entered the hospital itself with my wife. Some went to other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was it difficult getting to the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was. It was already towards the last quarter of the day. It was dark, the streets were damaged from the shelling. The trees had been felled, fallen, and we walked as well as we could, by memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation at the hospital when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation in the hospital was terrible. First of all, in the actual yard outside the building, the yard was crammed full of people. The hospital itself was in a very poor condition in terms of hygiene. There was a shortage of water, and it seems to me that the sewage was also blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How were you accommodated at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had worked in that hospital for ten years, so I knew mostly all the staff, so we went to the x-ray department and we found some blankets there, and we spent two nights in the dark chamber there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And these were the nights of the 17th and 18th,, is that correct, or 18th and 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night of the 17th-18th and the 18th-19th and 19th-20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you please, this might be a good time for a break. It is a good break point in the testimony, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We stand in recess for twenty minutes:

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, when we left off you had just described what the situation was at the hospital, and where you were staying when you were there. At the time that you arrived at the hospital, did you see any JNA soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time they were not there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when they did, in fact, arrive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they arrived at the hospital they were probably somewhere within the hospital compound, but officially we saw them only after Mr. Vidic had handed over the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was on 20th, let us say at 00 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So around midnight on the night between 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry your Honour, there seems to be some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering. A strange sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Some backfeed. It seems to be fine now. Thank you. Your Honour, it appears to be when the court reporter is typing, I think, so there may be some kind of overflow from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you mind if, in spite of this strange sound, we.continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is fine, your Honour. I apologise to Mr. Cakalic for the interruption. Now, you indicated that around midnight between 19th and 20th that there was a meeting with Mr. Vidic, and the JNA. How are you aware of that meeting taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
