utterances.text: On 19th November around 11.30 pm, I was in Mr. Vidic's room with Mr. Vidic, and we knew that the town would be handed over at that time, and I said that I would take part in the negotiations because we had special ID from the Croatian Red Cross, authorising me to negotiate, not right now, but generally speaking, that I could negotiate on behalf of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And are you aware of who was representing the JNA at this meeting with Mr. Vidic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, it is very hard on the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone came into the room, it was a major. And I saw, judging by the pictures, that it was Major Sljivancanin. He walked in with the lieutenant, Kuzmic, Bogdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I am sorry, I think we have to interrupt again because of the problem with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am afraid we have to break for fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cakalic, when we left off, you were talking about this meeting which had occurred between Mr. Vidic and Major Sljivancanin. Where did you stay that night between the 19th and 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Vukovar hospital at the x-ray department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So this is the same place that you had stayed for the preceding two nights; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the night between 19th and 20th when this meeting took place, did you have any discussions or any contact with Major Sljivancanin? Did you see him again the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the transport of the imprisoned at the Vukovar hospital to Ovcara, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened at the hospital on the morning of 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning some time around 7.30 or 8 o'clock, I cannot exactly tell the time, all the people employed in the medical centre were called to a meeting, and all the others who were not employed in the medical centre were asked to leave the hospital premises through the door of the emergency ward. People were lined up there. There were about 250 of us altogether there. We were supposed to take out everything we had, out of our pockets, and to show it to them. There were two soldiers there. One was Pero. I found out what his name was later because he escorted us from the Vukovar military barracks when we were there for a second time to Sremska Mitrovica. He was cursing us, everything he could, and he said that he would kill all of us if on our side there were not some prisoners who were members of his army. At that time, I saw two stretchers being moved away with two persons who were JNA officers, I think. They also had oxygen tanks and infusion on them and they were taken away in an ambulance in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did these JNA officers or soldiers appear to have been patients at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And they were patients at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like at this time to show the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 8, please, and if the ELMO could be turned on and he can display this for the court. And if the usher can bring it...... Mr. Cakalic, do you recognise this photograph, what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is an ambulance and the door on the left-hand side leads to the emergency ward, and also to the specialist offices. This is where we were lined up, in the area between the vehicle and Gunduliceva Street on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you would refer to the photograph which is to your right on the display and point exactly where you were located at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the vehicle towards the exit out of the hospital, towards Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And as you were lined up out here did you see Major Sljivancanin at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit later, when we were taken to the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And that is all for this display, I think. Thank you. What happened when all of you were assembled outside in this driveway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the wounded were driven off, I mean those of the Yugoslav People's Army, we were taken out and we boarded the buses. There were five buses there now, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, Mr. Cakalic, I am going to interrupt you. Before you boarded the buses, did anything happen to you while you were lined up outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. Were you searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that a few minutes ago, that we had to take everything out of our pockets and also everything we had in our bags. We had to show it to them. They checked all of it and whatever they considered dangerous, knives, razor blades, they took that away and the rest we were allowed to return into our bags or pockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who told you to get on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were soldiers, JNA soldiers, and they told us where we were supposed to go. I could have gone to the fourth bus straight away, for example, but he told me to go to the third bus so they were filling the buses according to a logic of their own so that is how I ended up on the fourth bus, or third bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And exactly where were those buses located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I show it on the picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it would need to be turned on again, please. And again you must refer to the one that is to your right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went out this way towards Gunduliceva Street, and to the left and right in Gunduliceva Street that is where the buses were. On the left-hand side they are about 30 metres to the corner of the next street and that is where the buses stood, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, all of them lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What happened after you got on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got onto the buses they were waiting for them to be filled up. The first, second and third left, and then at an intersection they had to turn around because they were facing the opposite direction and they drove us from Gunduliceva Street through the square of Marko Oreskovi than Hadzijana Street by the marketplace, the bridge on the Vuka River to the square of Matija Gubac, I believe it was. Then by Velepromet and the Orthodox church, then Kraseva Street, then by the health centre, then to the Sajmiste Street and then to the military barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to Velepromet being referred to the Orthodox church, was this the Velepromet warehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The management building was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the JNA barracks, what did you observe occurring there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these five buses were lined up, then the Chetniks and soldiers came. They mistreated us psychologically. They were pointing at various people saying, "I am going to slaughter you", in this way, "I am going to cut your throat", in another way, et cetera. Specifically speaking, Bulic Milos was attacking Damjan Samardzic. He promised that he would kill him, him and his son, and that is exactly what happened at Ovcara. One of them came to me and showed me a sign like this (indicates), that he would slit my throat. From our bus they moved on to the third and fifth bus, the fourth and the fifth bus, and an acquaintance of mine came up. He worked with me at the municipality. His name was Vlado Kosic. He had a degree in economics. He was a councillor to the president of the committee for economic affairs at the municipality. He looked at me, he smiled, and he said, "Emil, you are not on the right bus", I said, "which bus is better than this one?". He said, "Well, all of them are the same". I also saw his wife. I saw Radwoje Jakovljevic. His name was "Frizider". I saw Sreto Nedeljkovic too, from Bobota, who guarded the storage for ammunition, open-air storage. It was about 10 metres from the bus, and he said, "Well now, I am going to take you some place and I am going to exchange you so there will be no problem whatsoever", so this was a comfort. However, what was not a comfort was what Kosic answered. At that time I could not think about it yet, but when Ovcara happened and everything else, then I realised that he had known where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe what these men were wearing, if you recall, and in the case of Mr. Kosic's wife, what she was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Kosic and his wife were wearing clothes of Yugoslav People's Army. Olive green and grey. Tito cap on their heads, and a star on the cap. Jakovljevic Radwoje was wearing civilian clothes. This Sreto, who guarded the stores of ammunition, he was wearing proper military uniform with a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would at this time like to show the witness Prosecutor's Exhibit 20.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is not an exhibit yet. It has been only marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It has been marked for identification at this -- prior to now, yes. Okay. If this can be displayed on the ELMO, please, and perhaps if the lights can be dimmed just a bit I think it is a little clearer. Mr. Cakalic, do you identify -- I am sorry, do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the yard of the Vukovar military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And can you indicate on here where you were located on 20th November? Again, referring to the photograph at your right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to the entrance. We were placed here by the hangar. This is where the vehicles were, from one to five. (Indicates). However, later they told me that a sixth vehicle had arrived too, but I do not remember that sixth vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did you see these other people that you have referred to, that you spoke with at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third bus that I was on was approximately here, and they came from this area. They came here to the first, second, third bus. This is where I talked to Mr. Kosic and to Sreto Nedeljkovic, who guarded the ammunition here in this storage area. (Indicates). The fourth bus was here, the fifth bus here, and later when I talked to our other people who were in prison they told me that the sixth bus was approximately somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Cakalic, was there any type of provocation from the people on the buses toward those who were walking around outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did the buses stay at the barracks, if you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think until about roughly, of course I cannot tell you exactly, until about 2 o'clock, 2.10 or ten minutes to two. That was roughly the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a place called Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where is it located in relation to the JNA barracks, and at this point I am not talking about the office building which you discussed earlier. Again, if we can have the ELMO turned...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are talking about the Velepromet warehouse. When you leave it is in the same street in the direction of Negoslavci to the right -- no, not Negoslavci -- yes, towards Negoslavci on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And approximately how far is it located from the JNA barracks, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 200 metres. I could not tell you exactly, but somewhere around 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the buses left the barracks, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Passing along Sajmiste Street towards Negoslavci, then we turned off onto a side road that led to Ovcara. Ovcara is a plant of the Vukovar agricultural combine, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Ovcara before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What did you observe happening when you arrived at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very many civilian vehicles on the right-hand side of the road from the administrative building, almost up to the hangar. The first bus stopped in front of the hangar, and the prisoners started getting off, one by one. They were taken over by a captain of the Yugoslav army. I assumed he was a reservist because could he not button up his officer's blouse. He was putting his hands in people's pockets and taking out what he wanted, or what he needed. After that, we had to pass between two rows of Chetniks on our left and our right, and they beat everybody. I must say an elderly man called Bosanac, he is Dr. Bosanac's father-in-law. He was over 70, but he too was beaten with sticks so that he fell down. When the first and second buses were unloaded, then it was my bus's turn. I too came off and reached that captain. He took off my glasses, he tried them on himself. The sun was still shining, they changed colour because they are photosensitive multi-focals like these, so he tried them on himself. He saw that they did not suit him, he threw them down and trampled on them, and then I went in between the Chetniks and they beat us all. Before entering the hangar, maybe two and a half or three metres away, I was called out by name, "look at our inspector. So you are here too Emil, what are you doing here?", and I turned around and I recognised Slavko Dokmanovic. And I said, "I am doing what everyone else is doing here", and when he called me, "inspector", the people who were beating me probably thought I was a police inspector so I was badly hurt, and when I entered the hangar, the beating even intensified. When I got into the hangar I saw Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic too. He was kicking Dado... one of our soldiers. I cannot remember his surname just for a moment, who had injuries ton his legs and he kicked him in those wounds. I also managed to see him make a leap that is in football known as scissors, that he did that, and at that moment Milos Bulic approached me and with a wooden crutch he hit me on the neck, due to which I suffered a serious injury of my vertebrae and I think there is evidence of that here in the documents. By then we were all already covered in blood, and on the right-hand side, right from the entrance into the hangar, the prisoners were lined up with their hands against the walls with their feet as far from the wall as possible, and they were beaten. They beat them as much as they wanted and as much as they could, the people who were inside On the left-hand side, about seven, eight or maybe 10 metres away, I cannot say exactly, there were piles of hay. Somebody pointed at me to go there and I sat on the hay and at that moment I saw that something was really happening to Damjan Samardzic that was promised him in the barracks. Milos Bulic and some others had thrown him on the ground on his stomach. They were jumping on his back. They caught him by the hair, and he hit his head against the concrete. Then they turned him around, they jumped on his stomach. He was bleeding through the nose and the mouth and he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, if I can interrupt you for just a moment, you said that as you came in you heard this voice and then you recognised Slavko Dokmanovic. How do you know Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked in the same institution that I worked in. He was an adviser of the committee for agriculture and we met maybe 14 or 15 years ago at the Vupik plant in Bobota. I knew him also as the president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar. We would often meet in his office and elsewhere and we would greet one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And so you had occasion to speak with him over these fourteen or fifteen years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And prior to 20th November, how would you describe your contacts with him? Were they friendly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were friendly. And my last contact with him, I think it was some time in June, about a month after the massacre of the Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo, when a delegation was supposed to come to Vukovar and it consisted of a representative of the international Red Cross. I think his name is Dr. Nicholson, and then the secretary of the Yugoslav Red Cross, Rade Dubijic, the secretary of the Croatian Red Cross, the late Dr. Anto Dubosovic, the secretary of the Vukovar Red Cross, a lady, and myself as the president of the Red Cross. I was to invite the president of the municipal assembly to attend that meeting. I personally went to Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic's office, the president of the municipality of Vukovar, and I conveyed to him this, asking him to come to the meeting. As, however, Mr. Vidic came to the meeting, I think at that time he was still not a representative of the Croatian government, the envoy of the Croatian government for the municipality of Vukovar, and that was actually the first time I had any contact with Mr. Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Again, I think we have a bit of a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it is the transcript which is causing a problem. I apologise. Just one moment, please. Now, you have indicated that you went to see Mr. Dokmanovic to convey to him an invitation to this meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic did not come to that meeting. He sent Mr. Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But did you see Mr. Dokmanovic on the occasion where you had conveyed this invitation to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in his official office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was there any discussion with him at that time, any talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I invited him, I said, "Slavko, please be so kind as to come to this meeting", and I said, "who else would be invited?". There was no written invitation. I came to ask him to come in person, orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recall what his response was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he would come, and if he could not come for any reason, that he would send someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, do you see Mr. Dokmanovic in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I see him. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you describe where he is seated and point him out, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is seated in the last row on the second seat from the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused, Mr. Dokmanovic. On 20th November, do you do you have any doubt that it was Slavko Dokmanovic you saw at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I am sure I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall what he was wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a blue uniform, perhaps a little lighter than my jacket. On his hat he had the Tito cap with a five-cornered star, and a jacket. Three-quarter length, maybe 20 centimetres above his knees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dokmanovic hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you were beaten at Ovcara. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time that you saw Mr. Dokmanovic, what was your mental state at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in quite a good mental state, but I was terribly surprised. I could record every detail and I remember events very well. I only have problems with timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At any point during the day did you lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten, I fell down, but I got up too, because those who fell down, they never got up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was your vision impaired in any way during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wear correctional lenses but at the time I was without my glasses. The strength at the time was 1:25, 2:75; now I have 1:75 and 4, but I would describe each person in this room, how they are clothed and what they look like, even without my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At any point in time, was your face bloodied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was. That may be the reason that I did not recognise some other people, because blood was coming from my nose and mouth and this blood was covering my face and clothes, but after a short time I wiped myself off with a handkerchief so I could see well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the point you have indicated you saw Mr. Dokmanovic, was there blood on your face at that time? .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was it affecting your eyesight in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, earlier you were talking about Damjan Samardzic being beaten. You felt like he had been killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else seriously injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The same happened to a man called Kemal, already in the bus during the transport when we were being driven from the barracks to Ovcara. He was abused by the soldiers accompanying us in the bus, who said he was a Shiptar, that they would kill him. He responded that he was not. He said he was a Macedonian, showing his ID card, that his name is such and such, that he actually has a Macedonian surname and not an Albanian one. And he was also killed at Ovcara, in addition to Samardzic, in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the hangar at Ovcara inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps one hour, on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the hangar, what was the lighting like inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar had glass panes, windows below the ceiling. These opened inwards, and the light came from one side of the wall of the hangar, and from the other side of the wall, so that one could see quite well, and when one could no longer see in the hangar, an electric bulb was switched on which was attached to a electricity-producing device.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: A generator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like for the witness to be shown again in this book which has previously been marked as -- for identification purposes only -- as Prosecutor's Exhibit 20, and perhaps if the usher can bring it, I can turn to the correct page. Mr. Cakalic, do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What is shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the hangar with the agricultural machinery inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was that machinery there on 20th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Again, perhaps, if the overhead lights can be dimmed a little bit, and Mr. Cakalic, if you can point out in this photograph where you were located and where some of these events that you have talked about occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I should like to show you the windows. The doors were a little more widely open than now. We went along this path between two rows of Chetniks, we entered, and here on this side was Milos Bulic, and after I was called out as, "inspector", thinking that I was a police inspector, he started beating me. I fell about two times, and then I got up and walked towards him. I was terribly annoyed, I could not control my feelings, but surprisingly enough, he ran off, even though he was armed. Here on the left, another three or four metres away, Damjan Samardzic and Kemal were killed. When I got inside I saw Mr. Dokmanovic. Roughly here (indicates), and he hit Dado Dukic. I could not remember his surname. Dukic is his surname, Vladimir, known as Dado Dukic. I know him because I was a friend of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you would turn to the next page, please, in this album, does this picture more clearly depict the windows that you were describing in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 20. Mr. Cakalic, what were the circumstances under which you were taken outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many of us. We were all badly beaten, and abused. We sat on piles of hay, you know, the way combines make them after harvesting the wheat. After some time, a man was standing outside the door, dressed in the clothes of the Yugoslav army without any insignia on his cap with a white ribbon, I do not remember whether it was on his left or his right shoulder. He pointed at me and said, "you, you old man. Come outside". We were unshaven, and we really looked terrible. I said, "I will not because you will kill me". He said, "no, I will not kill you. Come and stand here next to the entrance to the hangar". By then all the buses had been unloaded, so I stood next to the door and he told me to wait there. I waited there, but the beatings inside continued. I did not see Mr. Dokmanovic any longer. He left the hangar, probably. I went out, and I stood next to the door, then some other young men went inside, and there

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) I said that he was probably a Serb. We were taken out in front of the hangar. I saw the soldiers who had escorted us in the bus to Ovcara were there and they were looking for money. One of us seven gave some money. I do not know who it was. It was dark by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave the hangar? Leave Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When we had all gathered there after some time we were called into the hangar, and there was a colonel and two lieutenant colonels inside. They took our particulars down. They wrote them down with the help of that bulb, and only after that did we come back out of the hangar and then we waited until a combi-van came to pick us up. I must say that before I had left, some other things happened in the hangar. A man appeared, a very strong, big man, maybe 2 metres tall, well-built, I think he had about 130 kilograms, with a large cap and a big cockade on it, with knives in his belt, and a major. I later heard his surname, if it is correct, Milan Lukic, and I learned of his name when we were driven for the second time from the barracks towards Negoslavci and I saw him escorting the convoy. He wanted to use an electric baton, and the Chetnik, the tall one, I do not know his name, warned him not to do that, "there are too many witnesses".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can just interrupt very quickly, I believe we need a redaction at page 79, lines 10, 11 and 13, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken in this combi-bus that you were talking about, do you know who was driving the combi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Mile Bakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is this someone you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him. He is a person who came under medical inspection. He drove bread, in a special vehicle, from the bakery to the sales outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did Mr. Bakic take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we got into the combi I sat next to him. He was driving, and to my right was a soldier with a rifle, and I think there was another soldier but I did not recognise him. He was not a prisoner. And the rest were sitting behind in the combi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Velepromet. In Velepromet, we were told to come out of the combi, and a man came up to us and I knew him as a merchant from Negoslavci. His name is Bingulac. He looked at me and asked, "uncle Emil, what are you doing here?". I said, "what all the others are doing". He recognised some others and at that moment among the soldiers who were escorting us, we were proclaimed some kind of murderers, killers, bandits, killers of Serbs, and when this shopkeeper, Bingulac, when he heard us being called by those names, he said, "I do not have any room for them. Take them to Modateks", so they took us to Modateks. This was a privately-owned tailoring company. There were many machines inside, and when we entered there were about 150 women inside who had been collected in Vukovar and brought there. They were placed to the right, and the soldiers escorting us, one of them went in front saying, "be careful, the greatest killers from Vukovar are coming", and then I heard from among the group of women somebody saying, "surely, uncle Emil and uncle Guncevic and others cannot be killers. That is impossible. We know those people from Vukovar, they did not do that", and then a soldier turned around and pointed a warning finger at her to keep quiet. Those women were taken away in three buses. I do not know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 21st, until about 4 o'clock, 4.30. A man was there whom they called, "Dedica", or "grandpa". I do not know him. I had not known him from before. He gave us certain assignments to do, to wash up, to clean and so on, which we did, and on 21st at about -- or between 3 and 5, I had no orientation in time anymore, we were called into a small room. It could not have been larger than six square metres. There were some benches and some cupboards there. He told us to sit down there. He gave us some fish cans and some bread and water, and said he would lock us up because the Chetniks could come and slaughter us. That morning indeed they came. Many came to Modateks to see what we looked like. A corporal came. I think he was Macedonian. They attacked Berghofer a lot. The soldiers beat Dudas and Guncevic. Berghofer, the daughter of my colleague who was a market inspector, she pointed a knife, put a knife under his neck, and this sergeant major said, "when I take you to Velepromet with my... then Topola will burn out your eyes with cigarette butts". So, they were quite an inquisitive people who wanted to come and see us. Among others, a director of a department of Borovo came. His name is Jovo Dabic, with whom I was a very good friend, and when I saw him coming in, we hid behind the machines. We did not wish to greet him, though he called "Guncevic" who was his colleague from the economics faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that you left Modateks on 21st. Where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Dedica, grandpa, had come from somewhere, he unlocked us. Another man was with him. He had the rank of captain. I know him, but I cannot remember his last name now. I am sure I will remember afterwards. The two of them escorted us on foot from Modateks to the Velepromet warehouse. That was a collection centre for the prisoners. There was a drizzle. It was quite cold. I just had this kind of jacket on, so we were poorly-dressed. In front of the entrance to Velepromet on the right-hand side of the road, there was a group of a few people who were wearing Yugoslav army uniforms and they had helmets on their heads and they kept yelling, "give me Perkovic, give me Krtinic", et cetera, and I recognised Pero Krtinic to be among them because we used to see each other quite often when we went fishing. However, this Dedica, grandpa, was very fair, and he said, "if anyone touches any one of these seven men I shall personally kill him", and indeed no one touched us. And he said, "when I hand them over, then you do whatever you want to them. Then it is your affair". We were taken to the carpentry shop. There was a hallway there and there was a room on the left-hand side and on the right-hand side. When we entered this room we were going in one by one, then we were supposed to put our hands on the wall to put our feet apart and we were searched. Everything was taken away from us. Everything that we had. If you remember, when we were getting off the buses, I mentioned that I only had my spectacles taken away from me but I had everything else. I had all my documents, I had my ID, I had that paper authorising me to negotiate on behalf of the Red Cross, I had money, I had my savings account book, and they took everything away from me. Everything I had, and what they did with it I really do not know. I saw a doctor there, Dr. Maric. He was an orthopaedic surgeon. We were very good friends. He was sitting at a desk, and writing down our names and surnames and taking our other particulars, and I remember not one of us but one of the other prisoners complained to Dr. Maric that his blood pressure was -- that his blood sugar was down because he was a diabetic and Dr. Maric gave him three or four cubes of sugar, he ate that and felt a bit better afterwards. Dr. Maric could not face me. I saw that he was flushed in the face. It was very unpleasant for him, I could see that and I was also embarrassed. We went into this room. We called that room, "the room of death". I saw many of my acquaintances there. When I went in, Mr. Karlo Crk, director of the Vukovar slaughterhouse invited me to sit next to him, and he let me take his chair and he sat down on the floor on some kind of blanket or something. I cannot remember what it was down there. Once we were there this big door, it was a big door, and it was latched on the outside, and every time when this big door was opened, when somebody's name was called out, it was a ceremony. They had to unlock it, unlatch it, and then somebody looked inside and said, "you. You come out here". Mr. Crk then went out and he never came back. Ivan Golac went out, and he never came back. All of a sudden, the door opened and at the door I saw a person dressed in a military uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army with a cap, full uniform, bombs on both sides and I recognised Zarko Leskovac who was in charge of the civilian defence in the Vuteks organisation with whom I had co-operated. I organised first aid courses. I taught first aid courses to members of the civilian defence, and he was always organising these courses, so we were on good terms. I believe that he was drunk, because I had never seen him in such a state ever in my life before that. However, after coming and going, Perkovic Tihomir's name was called out. He was taken out and brought back in a few times. Every time he had new marks on his face. The last time they took him away, perhaps sometime around 11 o'clock, he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, Mr. Perkovic was one of the people who had been taken from Ovcara with you, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, did there come some point in time when you left there and went to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: (redacted)I think that he was a witness here the other day too. After some time after midnight, through the windows you could hear the noise made by the Chetniks. They were singing, and allegedly they were going to the room that we were in and threatening to kill us, and there was a little window there and you could throw a bomb in through it. A captain came and he introduced himself by his name and surname but I forgot it. He said that he was a captain of the counter-intelligence service and he said that he came to save us, to take us to the Vukovar military barracks. He came on a bus. He said that if we did not want to go then the Chetniks would kill all of us, so that we should get going quickly. He opened the door and we boarded the bus and the bus could not ignite so we had to push it and perhaps we had moved about 10 or 15 metres and we saw this group which started moving towards the rooms that we were in, the so-called room of death, and these people wanted to kill us. But the captain took us to the Vukovar military barracks. This was the second time we were taken there. In the military barracks, we got out of the bus and we were sent to a big room. Perhaps it was half of this courtroom. Yugoslav army soldiers were there to meet us. They treated us very fairly. They gave us water, food, blankets. We thought that we would manage to get some rest there. However, as morning was dawning, more and more military policemen were coming in, and they would beat individuals there. We were already a group of some 40 people because all the people who were in the room of death came with the six of us. Perkovic was no longer with us. We were all taken to Velepromet. I did not say this before so now I am adding this to what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As the morning was progressing, more and more military policemen were coming in. A young man's hands were tied behind his back with a wire. His hands were injured. They made him swallow two or three bullets. I do not know. He was in the camp in Mitrovica with me afterwards. Another man, Vukalic, from the municipality, Mr. Dokmanovic knows him too, he worked in the finance department. He was badly mistreated. He was beaten a lot. He was near me. There were three or four people between us, perhaps, and other people were beaten up to too. Now, as morning was dawning, it was about 7 o'clock, a soldier walked in without a cap on his head, with his hair cut very short. He had a military overcoat on and he introduced himself to us. He said, "I am Vojin Misic, a Serb from Negoslavci, I am Captain Vojin Misic". I do not know if it was him or not. I do not remember ever having seen him before that and I do not remember having seen him since, but this is what he said, "Serbs to the one side and everybody else to the other side". There were women among us, too. And one of them said, "what am I going to do? I am a Croat and my husband is a Serb", and he said, "to the right-hand side", so the Serbs were on one side and we were on the other side. And then he turned to us, Croats, and he started speaking to us. "Listen you guys, we are going to kill all of you. We are going to burn you all. We are going to throw your ashes into the Danube, to destroy your Croat seed". I remember exactly that sentence and I shall never forget it. We all became fearful because we did not know what would happen. He allowed people to go to the lavatory two by two, and as one pair would come back, another pair would go. Guncevic - see above and I stayed behind. We were the last, somehow. I said, "do not go out there, there are a lot of Chetniks outside". We had to go out of that room, go through a corridor and then go to the lavatory. There were a lot of Chetniks who were waiting there to get hold of us. When this was over, a list was made, and through that hallway where the Chetniks were. One of them moved towards me and wanted to grab me, but the soldiers would not let him. We were taken to the bus and then we were driven by bus to Negoslavci. We spent two or two and a half hours there, or three hours, I am not too sure. We also had an armoured vehicle with us, and I saw a lieutenant of their army enter that vehicle. I think that he had surrendered to our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need another redaction on page 87 at lines 8 through 10. Mr. Cakalic, just moving along a little bit here, did you eventually end up in Sremska Mitrovica on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 7th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during that time, where were you housed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavilion number 3 on the second floor, room number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where was this pavilion located? Was it in some type of institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The prison in Mitrovica, the corrections house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And were you charged with any crimes during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there any allegation that you had ever done anything wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why you were being held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like all other citizens, however, they were very well-informed as to what who had done. I had said that I had volunteered to be involved in preventative medicine for the Croat army and for the civilian population of Vukovar, because all the doctors and medical staff involved in preventative medicine had left except for a colleague of mine, Ivo Kardun. I charged him afterwards with the duties at the hospital because there were many things to be done at the hospital. It was full of wounded people and he was in charge of providing good water and he was -- and food, et cetera, and he was a very good man and very conscientious. I was first invited for interrogation, I think on 14th January 1992 by Mr. Boro Savic. He was secretary of a political party in Vukovar. And Goran Hadzic, president of this political party and later president of Krajina, the so-called, "Krajina". They wanted to get certain answers from me. For example, who carried out mobilisation in Vukovar. I said, "the military police of the Croatian army". He did not believe that. He did not believe that there was a military police of the Croatian army. But it was organised quite well, and pretty soon not very many of them, but they were good, and then who do they mobilised? They mobilised -- he asked that I say who they had mobilised in the building that I believed in. "They mobilised Nikola Pekic". And he said, "who is that?", and I said, "that is my neighbour. The nephew of the retired general, Dusan Pekic", "and what they do to him?", and I said, "they took him away", and he said, "they slaughtered him", and I said, "no, I did not".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Without going all the way through this, I just want to ask you a couple more questions, if we can, about your time in Sremska Mitrovica. As a result of your time there, did you sustain any injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what were the nature of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first heavy injuries I sustained at Ovcara. That was part of my backbone towards the neck, my right-hand elbow, I still cannot clench my fist until the present day. I cannot lift my hand any further, and I am not trying to say that this is only a consequence of Ovcara, because I was also in two massacres in Mitrovica. In the second massacre in Mitrovica, which was dreadful, we had to take off our shoes and take off our clothes before that. I had injured my left foot as a child towards the end of the Second World War, and when Vukovar was bombed from aeroplanes, I ran and I wanted to jump into a yard and then I jumped onto the edge of a step and I injured my foot in that way and when we were supposed to take off our shoes then he saw that I had a bandage on my foot. I do not know what he thought and he started beating that leg and foot and that bandaged area that was injured until the present day I have terrible pain in that leg and also atrophy of that left leg. I can show it to you if you are interested. We were beaten there. We had to lie on our backs first and then on our stomachs, and they beat us. It was not the soldiers who were beating us during the second massacre, it was the police who were beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And these police are from which Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards we got to know quite a few of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, afterwards we got to know quite a few of them because they were working in that camp in Sremska Mitrovica. We were in touch with them. They would take us to interrogations and take us back from interrogations and they took us to clean rooms. They would open the doors and they would bring medicine to many prisoners who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where is Sremska Mitrovica located? In which Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we will now stand in recess until 2.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Cakalic, let us briefly review the period prior. You said that Mr. Dokmanovic, president of the assembly of the municipality of Vukovar, that you had a meeting. When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That must have been at the beginning of June when we were told that representatives of the International Red Cross, Mr. Nicholas and so on. After that at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened with Mr. Dokmanovic in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is, did he leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there for a while. After that he probably left. I did not see him afterwards, nor did I enquire about him, but according to rumours, he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the municipal assembly disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A representative of the government of Croatia was appointed for Vukovar. Whether the assembly was disbanded, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was that? Who was the representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were working in the hospital. Those two or three days you spent there, was a part reserved for JNA reservists, the wounded of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were together with all the other wounded of the Croatian army. There were no problems between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a special room for them or were they together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were together but I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were some people taken from the Vukovar hospital on 19th in the evening, afternoon or evening, and do you know whether any of them ended their life in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stanko Duvnjak. He was a plasterer, medical technician in the hospital. I cannot remember his surname. He was taken away. Quite a number of people. I did not see our journalist, for instance, in the hospital. He was taken somewhere as well, but it is a fact that afterwards they were at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Even though they were taken away on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some of those I knew were taken to Ovcara and they were identified from the mass grave at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, I am referring to people taken away on 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When the armed forces appeared on the 19th --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will get to that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They were JNA, et cetera, but it is up to you to answer my question. That is why I am putting it like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me put the question. The question is; what were the different formations that appeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, there were formations of the Yugoslav People's Army and when the Yugoslav army left, then regularly the Chetniks would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am talking about the hospital on 19th and 20th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the Yugoslav army did not want to let the Chetniks inside straight away, but after entering the hospital, this Stanko Duvnjak, Sinisa Glavasevic and Josip Batarelo, and some others whose names I cannot remember, were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Among those Chetniks, whatever you wish to call them, were there local Serbs from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were those people who were familiar with Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could they show the JNA all the most important features of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Referring to these three points, the hospital, the barracks and Ovcara, did you see Slavko Dokmanovic anywhere else except Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am referring to the 19th, 18th or any other day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us pass on to Ovcara so as to save time. You said that Dokmanovic hit a certain person called Dado, if I am not mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell me where Dokmanovic was standing and where Dukic, and where he hit him and how he hit him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was entering the hangar I already found there Mr. Slavko hitting Dukic Dado.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wounded in the legs and he was hitting him in the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We did not understand one another. At what place, in which place in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly behind that white sign when you enter the hangar, through the right door, then three or four metres from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So roughly in the middle of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, you gave an additional statement that the Prosecutor reminded you of. On the second page of that supplement, you said the following: "Because of the circumstances and the condition I was in, I could not see who Dokmanovic was hitting, but it was not me."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I said that I saw him hitting Dukic. You can find that in previous statements as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But it is a fact that you did not say that. I can read you your statement if the court wishes me to. In your first statement, nor in the supplement did you mention that you saw Dokmanovic beating someone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, even in the official note, I think. We can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If your Honour, Mr. President, you allow me to have the witness read both statements, then we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection? Thank you. (Pause). Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you wish the witness to read a specific line of the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you indicate to him the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have shown him that in both statements. I have asked him to find in either statement the place where he said that Dokmanovic was beating Dukic. You have two statements that have been admitted and you cannot find that in either. (Pause). Will you please look at the supplement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please read when you find it, that you said that you saw Dokmanovic hitting Dado Dukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not say that but it says that he and others were beating our wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you had already said that Dokmanovic was beating Dukic. I said that was not true because it does not say in either statement that you said that. On the contrary, it says that you did not see who he was hitting and this morning you said he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I saw him hitting our wounded and one of our wounded was Dukic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that in both your previous statements you had said that you saw him beating Dado Dukic. In your statement it says that he used the baton on Dado Dukic. You did not mention Dokmanovic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object at this point. I think the witness has answered the question and I think at this point he is just arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila, I would like to ask you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How do you explain the sentence that I just read out to you, from your supplementary statement, dated 21st April 1996: "Due to the circumstances and the condition I was in, I could not see whom Dokmanovic was beating but he was not beating me." Let him explain this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that when I walked into the hangar, that he was beating our wounded. Among our wounded, but it does not say that here, that Dado Dukic was one of them, but he was there and I saw him. I could swear to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do not swear, please. For how long were you looking at Dokmanovic at the time in minutes, hours, days, whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not counting the time, nor was I in a position to count the time, but I can tell you roughly. He was in my field of vision for maybe two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before those two or three minutes, were your people being beaten before and after Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we say then that the beating did not begin nor stop with Dokmanovic's arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you now explain in detail to us, describe in detail the clothes, or the uniform -- no, rather the clothing that Dokmanovic was wearing. Start from his feet, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not looking at his shoes. I do not know what kind of shoes he was wearing. I know he had blue trousers, that he had a blue three-quarter-length coat also blue, but maybe a little lighter than mine, and on his head he had a Tito cap with a five-cornered star.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I assume that he had a blouse, or a jacket, below that three-quarter-length coat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of material was it? Woollen, fabric or was it a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a blue uniform. The kind of uniforms that I think JNA pilots used to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that he was a lieutenant colonel of the JNA. He had his rank, he had the rank of lieutenant colonel on his shoulder. It is only us that know what those ranks look like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are worn on both shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do they look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three fields. The two end ones had a star, and the one in the middle did not have a star in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Over those stars -- let us be very precise. Was this on what he was wearing on top, on this coat, then, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this coat made like a wind jacket or was it a woollen material? A fabric, or was it a synthetic material like a wind breaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was woollen material.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, what else? What was Dokmanovic wearing? You said three-quarter-length coat made of woollen fabric. Thank you. You said he had a Tito cap on his head, with a red five-cornered star.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Whether he wore it afterwards, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We are only talking about those three or four minutes when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think it was in answer to a question from the Prosecutor that you remember events and faces, but not times so much. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that I cannot tell you exactly what time it is, when you are questioning me and whether something lasted five minutes or fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But do you know whether it was daylight or dusk or dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have already said that, and I will answer again, if you ask me a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am just going to. The moment the buses arrived, was it daylight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About after 2 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you saw Dokmanovic inside, how long after you had arrived was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two buses, I was towards the end, the last in the third, maybe this took about 40 minutes. Maybe about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So somewhere before 3 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you left the hangar, your small group, was it still daylight, or was it getting dark or was it dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came out it was still daylight and when some other people joined us, dark started to fall. We did not all come out at the same time. This took a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The moment you left the hangar, it was still daylight. The event with Dokmanovic happened before that, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After you left the hangar and it was still daylight you no longer saw Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that when darkness started to fall, an electric bulb appeared. Was there a vehicle around, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there was an electric bulb. I assume there was a generator because one could hear it. One could hear the sound, but we did not go to check. We were not in a position to check. The light was sufficient for the people taking down our names to be able to write them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see a vehicle with the lights switched on entering or facing the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were taken out of the hangar it came. A vehicle came in front of the door of Ovcara. It stopped right next to the road and I do not know how many, about 10 or 15 soldiers came out in uniform of the Yugoslav army with helmets and with baseball bats. They entered the hangar. The soldier on duty closed the door of the hangar. There was a colonel inside, and upon his whistle half of them, probably half of them beat them as much as they would and could, and when this officer blew his whistle again, then those who were resting took the other group's place. This was terrible. The screams. I dream them, you know, sometimes. I wake up with them and I go to sleep with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If that means anything to you, I believe you absolutely, personally. I quite agree with you. That is terrible. My question was, was there a vehicle that was lighting you up, not a vehicle that had brought some people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The combi made a turn there. Whether there was any other vehicle... it seems to me that perhaps there was a passenger vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, a military vehicle. Was there a military vehicle that was standing in front of you and lighting you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your supplement, you said that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic in the media and on television later. What year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in 1991 while we could still watch television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I am talking about much later, when you got to Zagreb you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him on television. I cannot tell you the day or the hour. I just remember the event, seeing him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that 1994, 1995? Is that the period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I saw him on television when he became a member of the Serbian National Council. There was a picture of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So I assume they took a picture of them. I have given the tape to the Prosecution. You will see that he was never a member of the Serbian Council, but when did you see them later on television? When you got back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him the other day on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I believe you. You saw me then, as well, but I am not talking about that:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I am talking about events, about all the events. I am interested in events and I am recounting those events. I am not learning them by heart to be able to tell you on such and such a day at such and such an hour I saw this. I am not even making an effort to remember such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But in your supplementary statement you said: "Upon returning to Croatia I saw Dokmanovic several times on television and in the newspapers." When was that, even two days after your return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I told you I saw him the other day again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But can you please tell us, was this 1995, 1994? When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, it was in 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you saw him at Ovcara that evening, did you hear him say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the afternoon, not the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right, the afternoon. Apart from anything, "inspector, how come you were here?", did you hear him say anything else? Did he give any orders to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps he was, but I did not hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, except for this phrase, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude anything about him regarding the JNA and everything else then, not now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was extremely astonished and it affected me. May I add a few words?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. I think if the witness has something else he would like to say then he should be allowed to answer it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise immediately. I was just watching the time. Please do say whatever you want. That is not the problem at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sorry. I felt embarrassed, in fact, that I had seen him there and I would have been happy today not to have seen him there because I was thinking how can an intellectual, a person with whom I had often talked in his office, who knew those people, I was asking myself how could he do that? If he had saved a single one, I would be supporting him today. I have heard that the man who saved me is an indictee. If I was in court I would testify in such a way to beg the court to forgive him. If Mr. Slavko had saved a single man, I would appeal to the court to forgive Mr. Dokmanovic, to pardon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know somebody called Vodicka? He was a vet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, he saved him from Ilok.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, from Ilok.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But we are talking about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have your views, I have mine. Did you see Professor Licina there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him at Ovcara? When they were saved and taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him in the bus, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was informed, I was informed that he was taken out of the bus at the barracks. You see, when we are recounting these things in the camp and elsewhere, he was apparently taken out in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Berghofer in the same bus with you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know where he was sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of me, maybe two rows in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you get off the bus when you reached Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I mean how, one by one or altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One by one. I will try to explain it a bit more precisely to you, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your statement, in your first statement you said that you were on the bus, and that you were sitting at the beginning of the first third of the bus, that next to you was a certain Papp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomislav Papp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. And a Josip Adzak and that you did not know anyone else on that bus.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I have known Berghofer for twenty or thirty years, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I believe you, but you said that you did not know anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, at that point, with that kind of surprise, I mean you would not have recognised me after half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not know what I would have done, I was not in your place. But you made a statement saying that you did not see other people. Now you say that Berghofer was with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could I say that I did not see anyone, there was a bus full of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I said that you did not recognise anyone and now that you have known Berghofer for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then how come you did not recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I did recognise him. What was I suppose to do? Give everybody's name who I recognised?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, there is also a recollection that comes afterwards. You know you reconstruct a picture in your mind, often, when necessary, and due to reality, reality, I talked about reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you something. When you were taken out of the hospital, what were the buses like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They belonged to Cazmatrans and also to the City Public Transportation Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Vukovar's plates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were red, red. I do not know whether they had that line on it, you know, their buses have that line on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understood you, yes. Red, and they had Vukovar licence plates. They were not with Zrenjanin licence plates and Skoplje licence plates, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They were not olive green, grey, but they were normal city buses, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a small thing which seems to be controversial. When you were going from the hospital towards the military barracks, did you go directly or did you go via Velepromet or did you pass by Velepromet, because Velepromet is behind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. My bus did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you about your bus. You had a watch on you when you were in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, but it did not occur to me to check what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. That is understandable. One more question. You mentioned a certain name, Golac. Was that Ivan Golac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is also a person called Krunoslav. They are two brothers, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is my last question. You said that Mr. Dokmanovic had the insignia of the JNA lieutenant colonel. In a statement of yours you said that perhaps he was a reservist and perhaps he was an active officer, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all wore the same uniforms, the reserve and the active officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Williamson, would you like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, how did you recognise Mr. Dokmanovic at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Dokmanovic for over fifteen years, for sure. And I shall probably recognise him within ten years' time if we are both still alive by then if we get to see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you recognise him because of seeing his face or because of the clothing he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His clothing even surprised me. I recognised him by his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, would you help me with this? You say that you worked, is it right, in the same institution as Mr. Dokmanovic? Which institution was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the municipal assembly of Vukovar in the administration. The administration consisted of a few departments for social services, health, culture, finance, et cetera. Those are two buildings. They are within the same compound. Mr. Dokmanovic worked as a councillor to the president of the committee for agriculture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was that in the same building as you worked or another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to work in that building, but after that the committee for social services and the magistrate judge's court were in the compound elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: During the time that you and he worked in the same institution, on average, about how often did you used to meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An agricultural inspector shared his office with him and I would often come by Mr. Res, the inspector, to see him, because we had assignments that involved both of us and then I would see Mr. Dokmanovic and we would say, "hello", to each other, we would exchange a word or two, and that was about it.
