Whether it was once a week or once in a fortnight, I really could not answer that now, but it was rather often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And during that time you would have conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would have conversations. We would shake hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And did you know him by his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he knew you by your first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, turning to the time at Ovcara, I know you find it difficult to give times, definite times, but I just want to be sure about this; can you help us, for what length of time, while you were at Ovcara, did you have Mr. Dokmanovic under your observation? Can you give an answer or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed him when he said my name, that is to say upon entering the hangar. Then I was beaten up there. I do not know how long that lasted but I was beaten a lot, you know? They hit me on the head and I would fall and I would get on my feet again and at one point in time when I entered the hangar I saw him beating our wounded. He was among these wounded and Dado Dukic was one of the wounded and I was very good friends with Dado Dukic and I was a friend of the family, I was friends with his father, Dado Dukic's father, and I was so shaken, so moved by that. Why did not I write this in the statement? I do not know. Perhaps I did not feel it was necessary to give the names of the wounded who were beaten. I said it in the plural, "he beat the wounded".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that, but again, can you give us an estimate of time or not, that you had him under observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two minutes, perhaps. Five minutes. It is hard for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The final question, which maybe the counsel can deal with better than the witness, what is a Tito cap? Mr. Fila, can you answer, or Mr. Williamson? Is it a side cap?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a four-edge cap, I believe. It is one of the narrow things that comes to a point, if you follow me, I know my hand signals may not be very illuminating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it easier to demonstrate than to describe?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your army, in the British army, they also had such caps. It goes this way, except that it was grey and it has a red five-pointed star in front. All armies have it. If you look at the videotape of the Prosecutor you will see Sljivancanin wearing one. That is it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I explain what a Tito cap is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a few questions. But first of all, do you think you could explain to us what, in fact, were the functions of the president of the Vukovar municipality assembly? It was not the legal structure -- not from a legal viewpoint, but in fact, judging from everyday life. I mean, what were the main functions of the president of the Vukovar municipality assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar is the highest organ in charge of the assembly. The assembly had very important functions; to work out the budget, to allocate it, to discuss the budget, to carry out various political functions. Also, to supervise all the individual departments and authorities. Although there was a head of every department, the president of the municipal assembly had to make sure that all the authorities functioned properly. He had the right to call me as the sanitary inspector to present a report to the assembly, to give certain segments. Very often I would attend sessions of the municipal assembly in order to explain certain health services or certain urban activities in the territory of the municipality of Vukovar. I do not know if you are happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you a question? For instance, I assume that there was a municipal police. Was there any police, local police, and who was in command of this police? Who used to issue, who was entitled to issue orders to the municipal police? The president of the municipal assembly or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police had their own chief of police. And all the chiefs of the different administrations, the different agencies, were accountable to the president of the assembly and to the assembly. The president of the assembly had the right and duty to ask every one of them to report to him on the situation in his particular part of the administration, his agency. The president of the assembly could also order certain measures to be taken. He could order mobilisation, and other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that between June and November 1991 Mr. Dokmanovic did not exercise the functions of the Vukovar municipal assembly. He was replaced by somebody else and you named his -- it was his deputy who replaced him, and he was a Croat. Now, do you know what role he was playing in this period, between June and November 1991, or what functions he was exercising outside his job, his profession? Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what other functions he had in addition to the office of the president of the municipal assembly, in the SDP, in the political party he belonged to. I do not know what other offices he held, but the office of the president of a municipal assembly is the uppermost office, the uppermost post in this territory, comprising some 80,000 people. He had a lot of work to do as president of the assembly. For example, the sanitary inspectorate in charge of preventative medicine and health care, we were very actively involved in the waterworks system. We had 21 villages and all villages apart from one had a waterworks system. The president of the municipal assembly had a very important function in this respect. He was supposed to go to various local meetings and explain on his own or together with someone else that it was necessary to build this waterworks system. That is one of the examples I am giving you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but sorry, I apologise again for coming back again to my question, but I understand from what you said before that between June and November 1991 he did not in fact exercise those functions because he was replaced by Marin Vilic who was actually acting as the president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar in that period, so my question was, do you know whether he had any other function either in Vukovar or elsewhere, in addition to his job, I mean, his normal profession. Did you know whether he was playing any role, political, military, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly when the government of the Republic of Croatia relieved Mr. Dokmanovic of his duty as president of the municipal assembly, but Mr. Dokmanovic probably held a certain office in the Serb National Council. This was on television once. It was broadcast on television, representatives of this council, and there are also books about that. They were written in the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the name of this book, the title of this book, but I know that I read about it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions about what happened in the hangar: now, in your supplementary statement, made on 18th June 1995 -- sorry, 21st April 1996, sorry -- you said that, and I quote: "The investigator...[the Tribunal's investigator]... showed me a number of photographs and I recognised Slavko Dokmanovic on the photographs L and M on the set number 2 and on those photos he appears wearing camouflage uniform different from the one he wore at Ovcara." Now, could you tell us what sort of difference existed between the two uniforms, the one he was wearing in the picture and the one he was wearing at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Ovcara he had the one I described a few minutes ago, and on the pictures he had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were in the hangar, did you have the impression that Mr. Dokmanovic was wielding any sort of authority inside the hangar, that is towards the people who were -- you call them Chetniks or soldiers, JNA soldiers, the people who were, according to your allegations, beating up various civilians. Did you feel that he was in a way above the other ones, that he was issuing instructions or giving orders or saying something which showed probably that he had some sort of authority, or was he on the same footing, as it were, as the other ones, either Chetniks or, to use your language, the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not call Mr. Dokmanovic a Chetnik. I do not think that he came there with some kind of authority to issue some kind of orders or something. I think that he came there at his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, all right, but I mean, how did he behave vis-à-vis the other ones who were there in the hangar, and who, according to you, were beating up the civilians? Did you get the impression -- I am sorry, you probably are a bit tired. Do you want to have some rest now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I am not tired. I am emotional, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I do appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you please repeat your question? Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but I will not insist, if you feel that you are emotionally involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can calm down. I can calm down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What I meant to say, is to ask you whether you felt, on that particular occasion that he was not as the other ones, but he was more -- he had more authority, greater authority, that he was above, as it were, the other ones, that he was in a way respected by the other people, who were there beating up civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I was the first to respect him. I do not know if other people respected him, but I did not have the impression that he was the leader there, that he was in charge there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again, while you were in the hangar, did you see anybody beat to death the civilians taken to Ovcara? You said they beat up a few people, including some wounded. Did you see whether somebody was beaten to death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Samardzic Damjan and a person called Kemo Kemal were killed at Ovcara right next to me. They were two or three metres away from me. I saw Bulic Milos killing Damjan Samardzic. I saw him kill him. I was not in a situation to ascertain all the signs of death but judging by what I could see from a distance, he was no longer breathing. Also Kemal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is about the general situation, before and after Ovcara. So you said before that you -- those days you came in contact, as it were, with, let us say, two categories of people; Chetniks or, say, paramilitary people, and members of the JNA. Officers or soldiers. Now, do you feel that, or did you feel that one group was in a way issuing instructions, giving instructions to the other group, say that the Chetniks were controlling the other group, or vice versa, or were they, again, on the same footing, acting independently of each other. Who was in command of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. The Yugoslav People's Army was the regular army of Yugoslavia. They had their ethics, and I imagine that many of them acted ethically. However, there was also a different situation there, that the JNA army came, and moved on further from that terrain and then the Chetniks came in immediately, and there may be a doubt, in respect of that, namely that it was agreed upon beforehand. I did not answer your question fully yet. I did not see officers of the Yugoslav army who were beating people up, but I saw members of the police of the Yugoslav army beating us at the military barracks when we returned from Ovcara. That is to say, that from Ovcara we went to Velepromet and then to Modateks and then back to the room of death and from the room of death under the leadership of a captain to the military barracks again, and then from the military barracks to Mitrovica. I did not see a single officer of the Yugoslav army beating someone, with the exception of Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, if you do not mind me, asking you another question? I am sorry, I see that you are a bit tired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At one point in your statement you said that you were saved. You were saved by Stevan Zoric, called Cevo? Is it correct? Yes. You say, "I was saved by a man whose name was Stevan Zoric called Cevo who remembered that I had done him a favour before the war". What do you mean by, "saving"? He took you out, but from what did he save you and do you think he was aware of the action he was carrying out, namely that he was singling you out and asking you to come out and be separated from the other ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the first moment I did not recognise Mr. Cevo, until he explained, and then my mind started working, and I had done something for him which a colleague of mine had not done, and I imagined he needed this quickly. Perhaps it was a paper, a document that he needed for certain purposes. Mr. Cevo saved me, and had he not saved me I would not be here today. Every one of the seven of us who were saved at Ovcara, we all had our saviours, Ivankovic, called Joe. He saved Berghofer, I think, and he saved...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do not worry. It is not important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. He saved at least two more people, and I am sure that they would have lost their lives otherwise. So we all had our respective saviours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much Mr. Cakalic. I am very grateful to you for answering my questions. I wonder whether there are any further questions or...

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further questions. We would, however, ask that he not be released completely yet, although we certainly want no restrictions put on his travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I know that I am not entitled to further questions, but with your permission, can we identify this person Stevan Zoric? Perhaps it would be interesting. Was his nickname Cevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Cevo was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Perhaps does he come from Montenegro, from Cev?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, sir. It is some kind of abbreviation. Perhaps you also had a nickname, perhaps you had a friend with some kind of nickname that you cannot really trace back, so I hardly ever called him Cevo, but in the statement I also gave his nickname, Cevo. I mean, he really deserves to have his full name stated in respect of me. I heard that he was killed in a traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Cakalic, thank you very much for coming here to testify. You may now leave the courtroom, and you shall remain here in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that the next witness has requested voice alteration and so I believe we are going to have to take a brief recess in order to implement that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, so we will have now -- how long do we need? Ten minutes? Fifteen? Yes. We stand in recess for fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, the next witness wishes to be referred to with a pseudonym, and to have the image of his face distorted, and his voice. Might he be referred to as, "Witness B"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration. WITNESS B (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, throughout the course of your testimony, we will refer to you by the pseudonym, "Witness B". Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like you to now look at the piece of paper that you are now shown and can you answer, "yes", or, "no", whether that is your correct name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could that be shown to Mr. Fila? I seek to tender that, your Honour, as the next exhibit number in order, and might it be tendered under seal?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness B, did you on 14th June 1995 provide a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal, Mr. Dennis Milner, in relation to events that occurred to you in 1991 at Vukovar and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was that statement taken down in the English language and was there an interpreter present, and did the interpreter read the statement to you in your own language, the Croatian language, and did you then proceed to sign each page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And would you now look at the document I now hand you, the document that is appearing in the English language, and... thank you. There is a translation of that. Perhaps that could be also allocated a number. Do you see the document in the English language? At the foot of each page of that document does your signature appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that if your Honours please, and might it be allocated the next number in order and the translation as A?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That will be exhibit number 55 and the translation, 55A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And I assume there is no objection from Mr. Fila. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness B, again, on 14th September 1995, was a further interview conducted with you by Mr. Dennis Milner and was a much shorter statement taken from you on that occasion by Mr. Milner and, again, was that statement reduced into writing in the English language and translated to you in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you now look at the document that I show you, please? Your Honours, we do not have a translation of this into the Croatian language at this stage, but I can undertake to provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, was this document provided to us? I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apparently not to your Honours, but it was disclosed to the Defence. But I can have extra copies made for your Honours. It is a very short one-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have not received it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Does your signature appear at the foot that have document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that statement, your Honours. And I have here three copies for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked as Exhibit 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness B, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you spend the most part of your life in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All my life, until I was exiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend your schooling? Where did you attend your schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I attended schooling in Vukovar. I graduated from the High School of Economics in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after you had completed your schooling, what did you work at? What was your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked briefly in the Borovo estate, and then I spent my whole career in Tranzjukrajke, the branch office in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the business carried out by that firm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an international transporter and carrier including exports and imports; in brief, international transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you live with your family in the city of Vukovar, prior to 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you then attend a specialist course for officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I attended special training course, and I spent a while in Pivka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you specialise in any particular part of military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The engineers, my speciality was pioneer engineers, which means fortification and mine-laying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if I may, I would like to take you to the commencement of military hostilities in the Vukovar region. Were you in Vukovar during the middle part and latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you -- during the summer of 1991 can you describe how circumstances changed in Vukovar in relation to the way of life and the military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is rather difficult to explain everything that happened, but obviously it is important from the present standpoint. The events in Vukovar on 2nd May totally transformed the situation in the Vukovar region, reflecting what was happening throughout the former Yugoslavia, including Slovenia and Croatia. In any event, with every passing day it became more and more difficult, or rather everything was pointing in the direction of a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, around about the 7th August did your wife and children leave the Vukovar region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They went for so-called, a holiday, or rather they were moved to the seaside for a period of three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did you stay on in Vukovar during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed, and I continued working on my house that was still under construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in September of 1991 did you take steps to participate in the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called to the municipal assembly building, and I attended a gathering to which the selection was made and appointments issued as to the assignments that would be allotted to people in the defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who did you report to when you went to the municipal assembly building? Who did you go and see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the younger Jastreb, Borkovic Branko, who convened the meeting on authority from Mr. Dedakovic and then secretary of national defence, Rehak Daniel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, these gentlemen whose names you have just given, were they military gentlemen or were they civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Borkovic was a military person. Mr. Rehak was the secretary of national defence, municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And dealing with the secretary of defence, was he related -- was he connected to the municipal authority, municipal government, or was he connected to the republican government in Zagreb, if you know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably he was connected to both. To both levels of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what military organisation was it that these gentlemen were associated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military organisation was called the Assembly of People's Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was that the forerunner of a particular military organisation that you can now describe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Briefly put, it was a part of the Croatian army, or the then Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the town hall and you discussed this meeting that was taking place, were you assigned any particular duties or tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned command of the engineers unit as part of the defence of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you to have any rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had a rank from before, from the former army, but there was no time or any particular need for ranks in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you to be referred to as, "commander", or how were you to be referred to by other members of this military organisation of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called me, "commander". It was a basic army unit. A commander and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have any subordinates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how many subordinates did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall we say eight, though the number changed, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you assigned any particular task as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My task was to lay mines where it was necessary under the direct command of Jastreb, Mile Dedakovic, or a young Jastreb or "Hawk", Branko Borkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you to wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not have time to sign up for a uniform because there was a shortage. The town was under occupation, and the remaining clothing that we had was saved for the killed officers and men, so all we had was military boots and we had HV insignia, or rather National Guards Corps insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this insignia worn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually it was worn on the shoulder, on the shoulder, but in view of the circumstances we wore them wherever possible, wherever we could sew them on. It was not ruled as to where we should wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you issued with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was supposed to get a weapon, but I was not issued one, at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you joined up in September, and during the period of September through October of 1991, where were you actually located, and what were you doing? What was the task that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were accommodated in the former School for Apprentices in the basement, and we carried out our tasks of mining and fortification building, depending on the decision of our superior commander, or Jastreb. And within the scope of the defence of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, from who did you take your orders? Who did you directly take your orders from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said directly from Jastreb, "the Hawk".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know who his superior was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know directly, but I can assume it was either Mr. Tudjman or someone else from the top leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you say, "Mr. Tudjman", are you referring to President Tudjman of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of carrying out your military tasks, can you describe the circumstances and what the conditions were like during the period September, October, through to November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that the psychological and physical conditions were extremely difficult, and it was all a matter of survival. It was very difficult, and one never knew what the next day would bring. This went on from day to day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did all the citizens of Vukovar remain in Vukovar or did some leave during the course of the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a difficult question to answer. Many citizens left the city. Some were coming back, and this was a daily occurrence while it was possible to come and go from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there reach a stage in November when it became obvious that the further defence of the city would become impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed to be that every day, though we kept fighting for as long as it was possible, or rather for as long as our command insisted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long was that for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until mid-November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened in mid-November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have mentioned, because many of the defence lines had given in under pressure of a superior force or they had to retreat, or were being destroyed; first a part of Borovo Naselje was cut off. Actually the defence was cut after which it collapsed , or rather the territorial links between various parts of the city were lost. After that, the headquarters was no longer in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the headquarters of the military forces just break up or did they disband and leave Vukovar, do you know? Or maybe you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to explain even today. I do not know because simply when I came on that last day or rather one day in mid-November when I went to headquarters, there was no one there except for certain individuals who had sort of got lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what did you do when confronted with this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Confronted with this situation, I returned to my men. I sort of disorganised them, or rather I told them what had happened, and I told them to head towards Vinkovci towards, freedom whereas I myself returned home to my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you mentioned mid-November. About what date was this? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably 15th or 16th November. I cannot give the precise date, because in that, those hellish conditions it was impossible to keep track of time and the hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were your parents at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My parents were in my house, in the basement of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the basement of your house with your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, before that, when I had joined the defence, so I was there until September. After the middle of September, I stayed with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: September or November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September. September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think that you told us a moment ago that the continuation of the defence of Vukovar ceased to be practical after about the middle of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that there was no sense, but we were simply disorganised. We lost our military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do from the middle of November onwards? What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, I returned home to my parents, and after that talking to them, they were probably listening to the radio or they simply heard the rumour that the evacuation of the citizens was being prepared within the hospital grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know when this was to occur? Did you hear when this was to take place, this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly. It was not stated with precision, but the word was that we should go to the hospital in the morning, so we were told that we should go to the hospital in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, do you know the morning of what day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am confident it was 18th November, maybe 19th. I am not -- I was not quite sure of the date at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, go to the hospital on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went there with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the hospital, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a large number of people who had congregated in the immediate environs of the hospital, between the old and new wing, and of course I visited my wounded men within the hospital compound who were being treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are these men that had served with you during the siege of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were the men who were with me in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are there any of those men's names that you can now recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes. Of course. They were my comrades in arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, if necessary. Darko Kalizan...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went there, apart from visiting your men, what else did you do? What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I registered upon my father's insistence -- as I had been wounded several times, I was entered in the list of members, the list of the wounded that was being compiled by Dr. Jozo Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And after you had registered with Dr. Tomic, what was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I went outside within the hospital grounds and I stayed there for a while with my parents, and then some military or paramilitary forces came from the city centre, specifically a major of the former JNA in an armoured vehicle with several members of his unit, shall we call that. They entered the hospital grounds through the main gate and this gentleman, this major, established the security of the facility. After that, I withdrew. I stayed for a little while outside and after that I went downstairs to the basement visiting other members, like Radovan Ilisin and some others, and that is where I was when night fell. I spent the night on the first or maybe even the second floor of the hospital, which was partly destroyed and the next morning we were called out with shouts and we were forced out through the emergency door, that is the gynaecology ward where the wounded and injured people would be brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who issued these orders and ordered you to go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people. I do not know. I cannot tell you who it was, but the message was passed on and there were shouts, and these people were passing by and conveying the message that whoever could walk, who were mobile, should go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this members of the medical staff of the hospital or was it part of the Croatian defence forces or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. Those were people who had come from the outside. In semi civilian clothes or with parts of military equipment on them, but it is difficult for me to answer your question now, directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I do not want you to tell me necessarily who they were, but did you associate them with the Croatian side or the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall we say the Serbian? It certainly was not the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you left the building, what happened? What was the next thing to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we were lined up in two rows. We were searched, they were looking for weapons or grenades or knives, I do not know what else, and after this search we were sent in the direction of Gunduliceva Street, the side entrance and we were boarded onto, or rather we had to get onto the buses that were prepared for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many buses were there? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there were three buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these -- do you know -- had you seen these buses before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are normal buses with 50-60 seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know what time in the morning this was, approximately, that you boarded the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could not have been later than 8 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to remember the date that this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeated the date. Probably it was 20th in the morning: I was not sure myself of the dates any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you boarded the buses, what was the next thing? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got into the buses we were watched by a soldier who had his gun pointed at us, the buses stood there for a while, maybe for half an hour, maybe longer, I do not know. I cannot tell. The buses were facing Borovo Naselje, which means in the opposite direction than it was normal in that one-way street. After all those buses had been filled, and after a certain amount of time had elapsed, the buses made a semicircle on the road. They formed a line, and they headed in the direction of the town centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, who were on the buses? Were they only people that had come to the hospital to be evacuated or was it a mixture of people who were patients and otherwise? Are you able to assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer that question, but those were the people found in the hospital. All those in the hospital grounds, or rather in the hospital building in the basement of the hospital or somewhere like that, who happened to be there at that moment. Whether they were regular patients or occasional patients or civilians it is hard to tell, but probably they were mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any guards on these buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that a soldier, shall we call him a soldier, had a weapon pointed at us, a machine-gun ready and he was looking at us with a threatening look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the soldier that had the machine-gun, was he a regular soldier or was he an irregular soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That can just be an opinion on my part. It is difficult for me to tell you what status he had, but he looked like a person doing his military service, a soldier doing his military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this is the military service with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the buses turned around and headed towards the centre of Vukovar, can you describe where they went to, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we went to the centre and we ended up in the compound of the former barracks, probably it is still the barracks. The only barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by that you mean the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the fairgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when they arrived at the barracks, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the barracks, this convoy of three buses formed a semicircle in the middle of the compound and since within the compound there were quite a number of people, crowds of people, who were, I do not know how to put it, they were circling around the buses, some of them were threatening, some of them were shouting, all kinds of things were happening, and then after some time another two or three buses joined us, coming from the direction of the fairgrounds, or rather the newly-built entrance, and what direction they had come from I do not know. I cannot tell. And we stayed there for quite some time, listening to curses, threats, insults, and after this time period had elapsed or rather two or three hours or maybe more, maybe less, it is difficult to say, the convoy left the barracks, and went out to the main road, and headed towards Negoslavci, out of Vukovar. Before Negoslavci it turned left to a road envisaged for farm work. It was really a short-cut that brought us to the agricultural estate, the co-operative for pig rearing and firms that engaged in other activities as well. We were led to a point in front of the hangar within the area of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, might the witness be shown Exhibit P20, please? I would like you to look at this exhibit which is -- on the overhead projector if you would for me, please, Witness B -- and I would like you to start with the first photograph, and just going through them photograph one after the other, and if you just say the first photograph, second photograph and third photograph as we go through, can you, with a pointer, trace the journey right through to the point where you reach the Ovcara farm? Can you do that for me, please? You will need to -- when you actually explain where you are going and so forth, you will need to speak into your microphone because otherwise your voice will not be picked up, so it is a bit difficult to do both, but I would ask you to bear with us on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken out here. This is the entrance to the surgery ward, and we were lined up in two lines here. We were searched and then we were sent under escort to Gunduliceva Street and we boarded the buses there. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness is referring to the first photograph in the booklet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I move on to the other photograph now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses were lined up on this side, if you look at it from here, and they were facing the back of this vehicle, that is to say Borovo Naselje. Actually, against traffic rules, because this was a one-way street towards the city. We boarded the buses there, and on this same road the buses made a U-turn and moved in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness is referring to the second photograph. Now could you move on to the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where the buses were. They made an U-turn, and they started moving towards the centre of town in a convoy, that is to say Gundeliceva, the square of Marko Oreskovic, Bozidara Adzije, down towards Dimitrija Tucovica. The next photograph. Further on Tucovica Street and then to this cross-roads, to the centre and then to the right towards Velepromet, Zmajeva Street, and then further on we cannot see much more, so could we move on to the next photograph? We went back to the street of Bozidara Adzije, across the bridge and towards the centre. As I said, across the bridge and towards the centre. The street of Dimitrija Tucovica, towards the centre, towards the right, towards Zmaj Jove Street and then further up. Towards the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness referring to the sixth photograph, now moving on to the seventh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are still in the centre of town. We are moving to the right, to Zman Jove, that is the name of the street then, I do not know if it is still called that. I am sorry, I am sorry. We are here, this is Zmaj Jove, and then up to Kraseva, towards the fairgrounds. Can we move on to the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now moving on to the eighth photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are still in Zmaj Jove and we are moving further up towards the intersection, towards Kraseva, towards the fairgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The ninth photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are still moving towards Kraseva, we are moving further up towards the fairgrounds. We can move on to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The tenth photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continue along Kraseva and move to the fairgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Eleventh photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an intersection, Kraseva and the street of the fairgrounds. We move further, on to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Twelfth photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the intersection. That is the Kraseva and the street of the fairgrounds towards the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thirteenth photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the military barracks. We came here from town and we turned to the left. This was the new entrance to the military barracks, and then we made a semicircle and the buses stood here. (Indicates). Three of them, and then at least two or three other buses joined the convoy here along this road, and after having joined us and after we stayed there, and were mistreated in different ways and threatened and who knows what else they did, what I did see and what I did not see, then we were driven back to this same entrance or rather exit and then we turned to the left, towards Negoslavci, that is to say out of town in the direction of Negoslavci, the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next photograph? I think we can skip the next two photographs, 14 and 15. The next one? The 16th photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the road that leads out of town and from fairground, and that moves towards the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Next photograph? 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the way out of Vukovar in the direction of Negoslavci. We turned to the left then. I am not sure whether this is exactly the point where we turned to the left, or whether it was an asphalt road. I had the impression that this is not an asphalt road, but at any rate, we turned to the left and we went further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 18th photograph, the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same cross-roads, but I do not have the impression that this is the right cross-roads. We turned to the left towards Ovcara either here or a bit further after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next photograph, number 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is probably the direction from which we came, and then we turned to the right, and continued towards the Ovcara farm, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Number 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Continued along this road, in this direction, and then to the left and then again a bit to the left towards the Ovcara farm and then to the right, to the right, to the hangar, to a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Number 21?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is it from a different vantage point. This is the road that we took, and the convoy brought us here, and stopped in front of the hangar, and bus after bus was unloaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is to say that we are already in the Ovcara area, and we are moving towards the hangar, and we stopped there by the entrance to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just leaving that there for the moment, and perhaps the exhibit can be left on the ELMO machine for the time being. Now, Witness B, you said that you arrived at the hangar, that you have just pointed to on Exhibit 20, and what happened then, once the buses pulled up at that spot, that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What happened? The passengers, so to speak, disembarked, one by one, and they did not really run the gauntlet. You could not see it here yet, but they were grabbing everything away from these people, everything that they had on them, their personal belongings, anything of any value, jackets, whatever. They were grabbing it and then they started mistreating them. People were forced to pile up their personal belongings on a big heap that they had on them at that point, and then they were taken to -- into the hangar itself where they ran the gauntlet. I mean, these people who were there to meet us, they were beating us with batons and all sorts of things they had in their hands. They had shovels, they had iron bars, they had weapons, they used their hands and arms and legs, whatever they could, and after that, as the buses were unloaded, then people disembarked and were in the hangar where the torture continued, and the mistreatment with greater or lesser intensity. They really mistreated some people and other people a bit less but it was hell out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What bus were you in, in the order? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I was on the third bus, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have a watch on your possession at the time when you got out of the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I still had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened to your watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I ran the gauntlet it was broken because I had received several blows. My body, my head, and of course my watch could not take all of that. It was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you hit -- you said, I think, that you were hit on the head. What were you hit on the head with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably an iron bar, because I received a severe blow and after that there was a big swelling on my head and after that, as I ran the gauntlet, I was hit several times and then I was thrown onto the straw that was in part of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who hit you on the head? Did you know? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. There was such a lot of commotion, such a lot of dust, it was impossible to notice anyone in that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did these people appear to you to be regular soldiers or were they paramilitaries, or were you able to ascertain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could only conclude while I was viewing it from the outside, as people before me had to put aside their personal belongings, as they had their things taken away from them, I could see that this was a group of different people. They were wearing different clothes, and it was a mob, to put it mildly. Also, with some insignia of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you recognise any people in this mob that you saw, that were hitting and beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to give the names of any of the people that you saw and recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With great difficulty. Before I disembarked I saw Dusan Borovac, called Dule, for example. He was a salesperson from Gvozdzara. That is to say, one of the local people who lived in Vukovar. At that point in time I saw him. I can say that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went inside the hangar, and you sat on the hay that you spoke of, were people being beaten in there, inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said so, that the terror continued with greater or lesser intensity. 10 or 15 or 20 people were going around in circles and they would question one person and then another person and torture him and beat him using all the resources they had available, such as rifles, for example, they would use a rifle butt to hit people. They even had baseball bats. They had some wooden sticks, not to mention that they used their hands and arms and feet and legs, military boots. Dukic Vladimir, called Dado, was heavily wounded in his upper thigh. He had wounds from gunshots and he had crutches and he had a lot of trouble boarding the bus and I do not know how he managed to get there through the hangar. They used his own crutches that he used in order to walk so they were breaking his body with his very own crutches, and as I said, they would perhaps beat the people they knew even more, or the people who said they were not from Vukovar. They were even more cruel and more brutal towards them because they thought that it was none of their business being in Vukovar, and many people were hurt very badly. One of them was very close to me and I imagine that he was killed as a result of the injuries sustained because he was even forced to sing the song "Sindjelic" and other Chetnik songs. As long as he had any breath left he had to sing and they continued beating him and kicking him, I imagine, until he died. His nickname was Kemal. I mean, the victim's name was Kemal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you say you imagine that he died. What do you mean by that? Did he appear to be dead to you or what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After everything, he seemed dead to me. He could not move any more, and I do not know what happened to him afterwards. He was very close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After all the buses had emptied out, about how many people could you estimate were in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to estimate and to be sure, but probably it was between 200 and 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone in particular appear to be in charge of the persons who were doing the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a big man in an olive green/grey uniform of the former JNA without any insignia rank. He was a very big man. He wore a moustache and he had a whistle. He used a whistle. He would channel the activities of the others and he would stop them or tell them to continue. I mean, these people who were committing all these atrocities, that is to say that he used a whistle as a means of communication with his subordinates, perhaps that is what we should call them but when they were maltreating people and going around, a few others held automatic rifles pointed at us and there was local Vukovar people among them, reservists, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you now look at the photograph, the next photograph in the booklet, there, please? On the table beside you? It is Exhibit P20 and the photograph you have to look at is the 23rd photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is shown there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the hangar, except that then it was without these vehicles, and it was partly full of straw, and the hangar had a few entrances or exits and this is the main entrance where we ran the gauntlet and where we were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you go on to the next photograph, photograph number 24?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to see where one is from this point. If the entrance is here, it is hard to say now, we ran the gauntlet here and we were thrown into the room at this point. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next photograph, photograph 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is also the hangar. As I said, the hangar has several entrances, so it is difficult for me to orientate myself where the main entrance was. For example, if it was on this side then we ran the gauntlet here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to people being beaten during the period of time that they were there, were -- was there anything else that was happening that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A list was made. How should I put this, of all the prisoners, of all the victims. There was a soldier, neat and tidy, in an olive green/grey uniform with a moustache, a short haircut, camouflage uniform, and he made a list of all the detainees, and after a certain period of time dusk had fallen -- night had fallen, most probably, because it was almost winter time, and some generators were turned on, something, that provided electricity, light, from outside. And in the meantime, as I said, they were going in and out, these people who mistreated, abused, and tortured people. And after night fell, after some time, people started going out, 10 or 15. They would say how many people should line up in a queue, and then they were taken out of the hangar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who ordered them to line up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers. Those who had weapons. I cannot say exactly who gave the direct order for that, but the soldiers who were there. They lined the people up and took them out, so, it happened every 10 or 15 minutes, as I said. They were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the men were taken out, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice it in particular, because there was a lot of noise. There was a truck or a generator that was on, so there was a lot of noise coming in from the outside, so I did not notice anything in particular except for that noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say the men were selected in groups of fifteen or maybe more. Was this selection, did it appear to be done on a systematic basis, or was it -- were they just sort of selected according to where they were positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not systematic, it was purely technical. They went according to the position that people took in the hangar, that is to say they started from the door, mechanically, not selectively, except in terms of numbers, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where were you positioned in the hangar, in relation to the door, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite far away, somewhere in the middle. Perhaps third, fourth or fifth group. It is hard to say, but in any event I was not among the first nor among the last.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise or know any of the men that were taken out in these groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to say. I knew the people right next to me that I really saw, but I cannot really say about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you say their names, the names of any of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were closer to me and that I recognised who were there, there was, for instance, Stanko Duvnjak, a policeman in Vukovar, Milan Greza who was a police inspector, Drago Krizan, Vladimir Dukic, Zvonko Jarenica, the young Zambta Slaven, Vukojevic, Damir, who was a driver in the hospital, Kemal, whom I believe they beat to death on the spot. Those are some of the names I can recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the time come when you were selected to go outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said maybe the third, fourth, or even fifth group, so I too was taken out, and boarded onto a military vehicle of about 2 tonnes carrying capacity with a canvas cover, and several of us were loaded on, a certain number. I cannot be sure about the number of people. But some of those people I know, that were around me, such as, for instance, Zeljko Jurela, Mato Perak, whom I knew well from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us by saying approximately how many people were in your group? I know you cannot be precise, but if you could just give us an approximation of the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we say about 10, 10-15. It is really difficult to say, because one could not at that moment focus on numbers and faces, but judging by the size of the truck, one can deduce how many there were roughly because it is a standard military vehicle of about 2 tonnes which has a certain capacity as to the number of people that could be loaded on. We were not too crammed, so there were 10-15, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you board the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We boarded it through the middle with the use of folding steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the weather conditions like outside? Can you describe the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night, night. But there was a moon so it was not pitch dark. The skies were lighted after all, were lit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you boarded the truck, was there any soldiers in the back of the truck with you or was it just prisoners in the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Just prisoners. After loading us, the soldier folded the steps and locked the entry as most of the truck was covered with canvas. And then they got on to the driver's seat next to the drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you sitting in the truck when you boarded it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hardly remember whether I was sitting at all. But shall we say on the left-hand side of the truck, looking at it from the side we boarded it, so when you climb up in the back to the left-hand side, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by, "the middle", you mean you were seated somewhere in the truck between the front and the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the truck have a -- any sort of flap or canvas covering on the back of it as opposed to the top, or was that left open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it was entirely covered with a canvas, even the back. Shall we say, about 80 per cent was covered. There was just a little space left for people to get in in the middle, so there was this small opening through which we crawled into the truck, after which the steps were folded and locked and the space was actually closed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having boarded, then we went back to the road we had come along, or rather we turned right in relation to the hangar, and continued our way more or less the way we had come, in the direction of the locality of Grabovo and after about a kilometre, a kilometre and a half, we came across a slope, downward slope in the road. The truck slowed down and turned left, on to a field road through a wood. This is marshland between Ovcara and Grabovo, and we drove further in a direction unknown to us. We were told we were being taken to another hangar that we were just being transported, and after some time one of the prisoners thought and wanted to jump off. Another one prevented him from doing that. He persuaded him not to. He was hesitant, and finally he gave up. At that moment I decided. I crawled through the space between the steps and jumped off through the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what happened when you jumped off the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I jumped off the truck. I turned around to see whether anyone was following me, and I headed towards Vukovar, or rather back, shall we say, in the direction of the hangar, in that direction, anyway. Anyway, in the direction of the town of Vukovar. And as I was moving away I would turn around from time to time. I was putting more and more distance between us, and as this was a valley I climbed up, and continued, as I said, in the direction of Sajmiste, for the purpose of easy orientation, and as I moved away, after some time, maybe a few seconds, or a minute, anyway not long after that I heard a short burst of fire, and a couple of individual shots. That was the last I heard, and I continued moving away, at times running, at times walking, or rather fleeing, in the direction of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to do this for me if you would, please. Would you look at Exhibit 20, at the last photograph, and I have also got another photograph here which I would like to have marked with the next Prosecution exhibit number, if you would, please. Your Honours, just to explain, the photograph that I am having marked now is in fact the same as the photograph shown in exhibit -- the 26 photograph, but would I like the witness to make some markings on the one I have given him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked as Exhibit 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness B, for the moment, would you just compare the two photographs and, for the record, can you just indicate whether they appear to be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And now, perhaps Exhibit 20 can be removed and would you put the single photograph on the ELMO machine for me, please? I think you will find there a blue coloured -- that can be handed back to the Registrar, the original exhibit. (Handed). On the machine table in front of you I think you might see a blue-coloured Texter pen. Would you be so kind as to mark on that by drawing with the pen, the route that you followed in the vehicle, stopping firstly at the point where the dip in the road is. Can you do that for us, and explaining as you go along your journey that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The dip starts here. The lowest point is here, and then it starts climbing again. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps to assist your Honour, if the lights could be dimmed slightly, I think we might get a better view of it, and if we can move that into the centre of the screen, more; now, I want you to actually start at the hangar where your vehicle, you boarded the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar is here. (Witness marks photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mark it heavily so it makes it very clear. Is that the point where the road dips? Can you just put a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- an X at the point where the road dips?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere here, shall we say. (Witness marks photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where does the field road start? Can you indicate that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where it stops? Where it starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where it starts, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here. It starts here. This is the road and here it becomes a field road. You can see it going through the woods. (Witness marks photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay, if you would mark that, please, the route of the field road, to the point where you jumped off the vehicle, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe like this. Maybe here. (Witness marks photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you jumped off the vehicle, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started running and climbing up and I continued running and fleeing towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. That photograph can now be returned. I have here a map of the area I would ask you to look at for me too, please, and perhaps that might be numbered the next exhibit number in order. I have a copy for the Defence of that. That should be made available to them. This is a map that has already previously been provided to the Defence but it is an expanded version of it. Now, again, Witness B, I would ask you to put that on the screen to orientate yourself to the map, and this time I would like you to do a little more for me, if you would. Would you please, as best you can, trace the whole of the journey out to Ovcara and then to the point where approximately you leave the vehicle and then the route that you followed in the course of your escape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. With the blue marker?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. As you are doing that, you might just describe what you are doing: If you cannot be precise in Vukovar, do not be concerned about that. Just do it in a general way and perhaps be more precise when you reach the country roads.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- let us say that the hospital is here then we went down to the centre via the fairgrounds. Here somewhere is the barracks, then from the barracks in the direction of Negoslavci, here, somewhere here, before Negoslavci, Negoslavci, the road turns off to the left, then the right, then this is the hangar. This is where we were unloaded. After that, the transport started. The depression, the dip, then the field road and I jumped off here somewhere; and I started retracing my steps towards Vukovar. (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could do that in broken dotted lines it might be a little easier, just so that we know, as you trace your trip back. As you are tracing your trip back from the point where you are now, if you just break the lines with broken lines it will indicate the return trip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I have already started, but never mind. I shall break the line now. Through the little wood, through the corn, the fairgrounds, I crossed the road, then I took the Petrovacki Drum road, then the road to Bogdanovci, left on Bogdanovci, then again in the direction of Vinkovci. And on towards Vinkovci, and I reached a village which I thought was Ceric. I had almost passed it, and as I was dehydrating, and after this long march, if I can call it that; I retraced my steps and found a shelter and I woke up some reservists, probably of the JNA, and I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I now tender both those exhibits, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 57 and 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you were captured by the reservists, what was the next thing that happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rest of that night I spent in a room in that building where they were staying, and in the morning they took me, they drove me to their headquarters, somewhere in the centre of the village, and of course they discussed what to do with me. In the meantime, some reservists spoke to me. They would hit me now and then. They took a gold coin that I still had in my pocket that my father had given me before leaving. They found it. They hit me in the eyebrows so I started bleeding a little. I did not spend a lot of time there waiting to see what would happen. Then they put me on a truck again and transported me to Stari Jankovci. Again, in a house which had been transformed into some kind of a headquarters. I was put up in a basement. I was beaten there as well as the others who were there. They were prisoners from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you interrogated during this time at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime we were, or rather I was, taken for interrogation by a captain who interrogated me, asking about my activities during the war, and after some time I was returned to the basement and then up, then down, and this went on, and then I spent another night there. I was -- he moved me to a room, attached me to the radiator with handcuffs. I spent the night there and then the next night, together with the others who were in the basement, I was put on a combi-van and transported to Sid, to the police station in Sid. There we were thrown or put into a small room and after some time we were taken individually, each one of us for interrogation. Again, there were questions as to what had happened during the war, who did what, and after --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from what had happened during the war, were you questioned about anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked all kinds of things. Everything I knew, what had been happening. He mentioned also Ovcara. Everything that he could think of, anything that occurred to him and after this relatively short interrogation I was returned to the room and then shortly some men came who took us out and beat us with their hands and legs and then like that they boarded us onto another truck and they drove us off. Later we realised that we had been transported to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. We were searched once again there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping for a moment, when you were questioned about Ovcara, can you remember what was asked of you about Ovcara when you were in Sid? What did they say to you about Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked what I knew about Ovcara, how many people had been killed and whether anyone had been killed. I simply did not want to discuss that matter with that man, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
