utterances.text: Did you gain an impression of whether or not he was aware of what had happened at Ovcara, from what he said, from the questions that he asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was that he was looking for information, whether anything was known about Ovcara, but since I did not show any interest in discussing this topic, we went on to other topics, and then he sent me back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you feel that you may have been in danger if you discussed Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I was constantly in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then you went to Sremska Mitrovica and how long were you retained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there from, shall we say, 22nd of November 1991 right through 4th February 1992, but on 15th January, after interrogation, and when detention was ruled by judgement of the military court, I was transferred to isolation where I stayed until 4th February when I was transferred to the military investigative prison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you got to Belgrade, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were accommodated. I was not alone. We were transferred to various cells. Most often there were eight to a cell and we were mixed; reservists and other members of the Yugoslav army who had committed a crime or an offence such as burglary or murder, and other things that had happened in their army. Most frequently avoiding mobilisation and other problems of that kind, so we were put up together with these people into cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you charged with any crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was charged with armed revolt and crime against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you come to learn of any evidence that was used against you in relation to these charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no arguments nor was there any evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, face trial for these charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The trial was scheduled for one date and then it was postponed. In the meantime the international community through my relatives and especially my wife, learned about my case. They realised what was happening and what was being done to us, and Amnesty International was informed and Mr. Paul Miller came to one of the scheduled hearings and after that it was postponed, I believe, because of his presence. Then again it was scheduled on several occasions, the hearings, but outside the protocol at the time, it was postponed and finally it was partially carried out with the exception of the closing statement of my Defence counsel and the pronouncement of judgement, it was never completed, at least I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you then subsequently released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were exchanged, as it was called, on 14th August 1992 in Nemetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, sometime later in August of 1992, did you meet with a gentleman by the name of Dr. Clyde Snow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at this meeting -- was this a meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Belgrade. After my release or exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I meant Zagreb. Yes. In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And at that meeting did you provide him with certain information similar to that which you have provided to the court today, in relation to the route that the truck that you were on took at the Ovcara farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave him all the facts that I have given you now in greater or lesser detail. Anyway, I told him whatever he asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, it is too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whatever you say. I only have three questions. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, will you tell us what kind of uniforms you saw, from the hospital to Ovcara and from then on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw various uniforms, if we can call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That too is a good question, but the answer is different. A uniform means that people should be equally dressed, but in this case, people wore different clothing. There were all types of uniforms from camouflage to classical, grey, olive green, and then there were those who were not completely clothed in uniform. They had a mixture of regular clothing and uniforms. Then there were cockades and other insignia. Olive green and inadequate uniforms and mixtures, all kinds of things. All kinds of combinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that Vladimir Dukic was beaten -- you call him Dado, a nickname. Never mind. Where was he in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was on the opposite side to the entrance. Not that close to me, about 10 metres away from me, but at that point in time I could see him from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know who beat him? Was he lying? Was he standing when he had these crutches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not stand up. He was heavily wounded. He was lying most of the time but he was sitting too next to the hangar door and he had crutches with him. He had crutches right next to him that were used to beat him up..

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You do not know who beat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army that guarded us, if that is what we can call it, and all the others who took part in this terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the moment they took you out, you said it was dark. Did you perhaps notice how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice a single bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when you were taken away, what buses were there? Civilian, military, and what colour, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, when we were driven off?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I mean from the hospital into the military barracks and all that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the hospital, did I not look at the registration plates. No, I did not look at the registration plates at that point. It did not seem to matter. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what colour were they? Were they civilian or military buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were civilian buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lighter colour. I do not know about the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know at all how many buses there were in front of Ovcara altogether? You said that you were on the third bus. Were there any more buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since we were joined by an additional two or three buses, I cannot be sure, but most probably there were six buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And as you were getting in, I mean, did you go out and then the buses arrived or were the buses there when you came out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One bus was emptied out after the other. That is to say one was emptied out and then the other one came one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you say what time it was when you arrived in Ovcara, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the afternoon. I do not know. Perhaps around 2 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 1400 hours. Something like that. But approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, thank you. No objection to the witness being released, therefore? No. Good. I imagine that tomorrow we will hear five witnesses, or some of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the five witnesses are ready for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good, and do you think tomorrow we could receive also from you the list of witnesses to be heard next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is what I was about to address. We are still in the process of finalising travel arrangements, so that is the reason that we have not provided it today, but we should have it first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good. So we take a recess until tomorrow morning at 9.15.
